header.exam_format: 25 MCQ, 4 options, 2 marks each, negative marking (-1 per wrong answer), 75 min. (Option count & negative marking confirmed by student 2026-06-03; PROMPT.md corrected to v1.2.1.)
header.style_profile: Distilled from the CLA (source/cla/ger.docx), an edX-style graded quiz (1 mark/question). The CLA is a roughly 50/50 MIX of (a) CONCEPTUAL/legal single-best-answer MCQs - incorporation forms & liability, separate legal identity, MOA vs AOA, DPIIT/DSC/AGM, trademark/design/patent/copyright, Category I AIF, term-sheet (non-binding, no-shop), information/anti-dilution/liquidation-preference/economic rights, investment-process sequence, finance function - and (b) CALCULATION items that map exactly to Modules 1-4: pre/post-money valuation, %-stake = investment/post-money, exit multiple = (stake x exit val)/investment, required-stake = investment x (1+r)^n / exit-equity, P/B = price/BVPS, EV = equity+debt-cash, net cash burn = payments-receipts, total funding = peak operational cash deficit + CapEx, liquidation-preference payout (participating = multiple + pro-rata; non-participating = max(multiple, convert)), and full-ratchet anti-dilution cap tables that must sum to 100%. Stems are often scenario-first ('An investor invests Rs X for Y% stake...'), with numeric distractors built from named mistakes (swapping pre/post money, dividing by pre- instead of post-money, using raw investment instead of realisation, forgetting the participation add-on, mis-reversing dilution). Question types also include Roman-numeral multi-statement ('I, III and IV') and matching ('1-i, 2-ii') items. Every distractor should map to a specific misconception, not a random number; for every calculation node the 'correct' value is one this build script computed and validated against the Section 4 seven-point cap-table checklist.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: In a start-up the finance function does far more than raise money: (1) it raises capital and ensures availability of resources for the business; (2) it keeps the CAPITAL PROVIDERS (equity shareholders, lenders) satisfied; (3) it measures and monitors PERFORMANCE on metrics appropriate to the organisation and communicates results to stakeholders; and (4) it designs INCENTIVE mechanisms (e.g. linking performance to payouts/ESOPs). The course frames financing as an ongoing RELATIONSHIP among three constituencies — founders, capital providers and the company — that must work in harmony.

distractors.wrong: The finance function's only job is to raise money
distractors.why: it also keeps capital providers satisfied, measures performance and designs incentives

distractors.wrong: Capital providers means only customers/employees
distractors.why: capital providers are equity shareholders and lenders who fund the business

nodes.sample_question: List the responsibilities of the finance function in a start-up beyond raising capital. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Reducing finance to fundraising and ignoring performance measurement and incentives.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Capital takes several forms: FINANCIAL capital (money), INTELLECTUAL capital (the professional's training/experience), RELATIONSHIP capital (network of relationships), and REPUTATIONAL capital (a track record that makes people want to work with you). The course focuses on financial capital, but a key insight is that a founder who forgoes salaried employment to start up is themselves a CAPITAL PROVIDER to their own enterprise (contributing intellectual capital and foregone compensation).

distractors.wrong: Capital means only money/financial capital
distractors.why: capital also includes intellectual, relationship and reputational forms

distractors.wrong: Founders contribute no capital until they put in cash
distractors.why: founders contribute intellectual capital and foregone compensation — they are capital providers to their own venture

nodes.sample_question: Name the forms of capital a founder brings to an enterprise besides money. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Equating capital purely with cash and ignoring intellectual/relationship/reputational capital.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Why a founder starts up shapes their FINANCIAL STRATEGY (where to raise money, how much, on what terms). Motivations span: serving SOCIETY (social enterprise/cooperatives), LIVELIHOOD/gainful employment (humble to grand), LIFESTYLE entrepreneurship (a less-hurried life), maximising RETURNS to capital providers (risk-adjusted market rate), and SELF-ACTUALISATION (passion, e.g. an art studio). Different motivations imply different speed of growth and funding needs.

distractors.wrong: Profit maximisation is the only legitimate start-up motivation
distractors.why: society, livelihood, lifestyle, returns and self-actualisation are all legitimate motivations

distractors.wrong: Motivation has no bearing on financing
distractors.why: purpose drives financial strategy — where/how much/on what terms to raise

nodes.sample_question: How does a founder's motivation for starting up influence their financial strategy? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming every founder optimises for returns/growth, ignoring lifestyle/social/livelihood motives.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Start-ups develop in PHASES, which (a) lets founders focus, (b) limits money raised (less dilution), and (c) resolves INFORMATION ASYMMETRY: founders know the technology/science, investors know how to deploy capital — staging reveals information gradually so each funding commitment is better-informed. Glucotrak illustration: Phase 1 (months 0-12, firm up manufacturing + pre-commercial field testing, ~Rs 5 cr); Phase 2 (months 13-36, early commercialisation / product-market fit, ~Rs 20 cr); Phase 3 (months 36-60, scale across geographies/products, ~Rs 50 cr).

distractors.wrong: Phasing is just an operational convenience
distractors.why: it also limits dilution and resolves founder-investor information asymmetry by revealing information gradually

distractors.wrong: Investors prefer to commit all capital upfront
distractors.why: staging lets each commitment be better-informed after the prior phase's learning

nodes.sample_question: Why do start-ups raise capital in phases rather than all at once? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Missing the information-asymmetry and dilution rationale for staged funding.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: The NATURE of risk changes as a venture evolves, so investors specialise by stage. Phase 1 risk is product development / product-market fit / supply-chain / reliability (a management-light, technical phase). Phase 2 adds market-acceptance and business-model risk (B2B/B2C/B2B2C) and needs managerial bandwidth; unit economics start to show. Phase 3 is growth/expansion risk (new geographies, talent, competition). Early-stage investors specialise in product/market risk; growth-stage investors in scaling, senior hires and incentivisation. Investors also work to fixed-life funds and need an EXIT within ~3-8 years.

distractors.wrong: Risk is the same throughout a venture's life
distractors.why: risk shifts from product/market-fit early to market-acceptance then growth/competition — investors specialise by stage

distractors.wrong: One investor profile suits every stage
distractors.why: early-stage vs growth-stage investors manage different risks and add different value

nodes.sample_question: How does the nature of venture risk change from phase to phase? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating venture risk as static rather than stage-dependent.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Start-ups differ from established firms. ADVANTAGES: high innovativeness/competitive edge, high growth potential, fast decision-making (no hierarchy/board to navigate), ability to learn from best practices and use new business models. VULNERABILITIES (liabilities of newness/smallness/novelty): small SIZE (low resilience, high mortality), lack of AGE/maturity, the liability of NOVELTY (customers don't know how to use/trust the product, slow adoption), and difficulty attracting resources (human, manufacturing, financial) — a large incumbent can cross-subsidise and price you out.

distractors.wrong: Start-ups are vulnerable only because they are small
distractors.why: they also face liabilities of newness (no track record) and novelty (low adoption/trust)

distractors.wrong: Being innovative is purely an advantage
distractors.why: novelty is also a LIABILITY — users don't know how to use/trust a new product, slowing adoption

nodes.sample_question: Give two advantages and two vulnerabilities of an early-stage venture vs an established firm. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Seeing novelty/innovation only as an asset, missing the liability-of-newness/novelty risks.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.concept: Sources of risk in early-stage enterprises
nodes.teaching_note: Standard sources of risk in early-stage equity financing: (1) TECHNOLOGY risk (does the technology stabilise/work?); (2) CUSTOMER-ACCEPTANCE risk (even a great product needs buyers); (3) INCOMPLETE MANAGEMENT TEAM (one-two founders, missing functions — no sales/manufacturing); (4) lack of production/marketing RESOURCES (must build or rent channels); (5) REGULATORY uncertainty (e.g. RBI on Buy-Now-Pay-Later, state rules on ride-hailing); (6) FINANCIAL-FORECAST uncertainty (forecasts can't be fully relied on — a 2017 NBER/HBR study found ~30% of early-stage investors don't use financial forecasts, betting on the idea/market).

distractors.wrong: Early-stage investors rely heavily on financial forecasts
distractors.why: forecasts are unreliable; ~30% of early-stage investors don't use them, betting on idea/market

distractors.wrong: The main risk is always the technology
distractors.why: customer acceptance, incomplete teams, resources and regulation are equally important risk sources

nodes.sample_question: List the main sources of risk in an early-stage enterprise. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Over-focusing on technology risk and ignoring team/regulatory/forecast risk.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Kerr & Nanda ('Financing New Ventures') map businesses on two axes: X = technology/business-model NOVELTY (low-high), Y = CAPITAL INTENSITY (low-high). Four quadrants: low-novelty/low-capital (kirana shop, notebook maker — personal/bank credit); low-novelty/high-capital (auto-parts manufacturing — bank/conventional finance); high-novelty/high-capital (space, drug development ~$3bn — hardest to fund, the 'valley of death'); high-novelty/low-capital (Glucotrak, Forus — the typical VC-backed quadrant: novel but needs only crores, not hundreds of millions). Q-commerce (Zepto/Swiggy) loosely fits the high-novelty/low-capital quadrant.

distractors.wrong: Venture capital targets the high-capital-intensity quadrant
distractors.why: VCs typically back the high-novelty/LOW-capital quadrant; very high-capital novel ventures hit the 'valley of death'

distractors.wrong: All novel businesses need huge capital
distractors.why: many high-novelty businesses (Glucotrak, Forus) reach commercial potential on modest capital

nodes.sample_question: On which two axes does the Kerr-Nanda framework classify ventures, and which quadrant do VCs typically back? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing novelty with capital intensity, or placing VC in the wrong quadrant.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Two basic financing buckets. DEBT/loans: borrower promises periodic INTEREST + repayment of PRINCIPAL, often secured (mortgage); legally enforceable (notice -> court -> insolvency); less risky for the lender, who is repaid regardless of profits. EQUITY share capital: participates symmetrically in RISK and REWARD — if the venture succeeds the investor shares the upside; if it fails the investor writes off the investment. Lenders are reluctant to fund risky start-ups except against a security package, so equity is the dominant start-up instrument. Hybrids combine both.

distractors.wrong: Debt is the ideal way to finance a risky start-up
distractors.why: debt's fixed obligations are dangerous for risky start-ups; equity (risk-sharing) is preferred

distractors.wrong: Equity is cheaper than debt because there's no interest
distractors.why: equity is not 'free' — it gives away ownership, wealth-share and control

nodes.sample_question: Contrast debt and equity on risk-sharing and the lender/investor's claim. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Recommending debt for a risky start-up, or thinking equity is costless.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Hybrids combine debt and equity properties. The classic example is PREFERENCE share capital: like a loan it is lent for a fixed period and REDEEMED, and pays a predetermined DIVIDEND (like interest); but it is share capital, not debt. Convertible instruments (convertible preference shares / convertible debentures / convertible loans) are hybrids intended to convert into equity. Hybrids let parties tune tax, balance-sheet and regulatory treatment.

distractors.wrong: Preference capital is pure equity
distractors.why: it is a HYBRID — fixed dividend and redeemable like a loan, but share capital

distractors.wrong: Hybrids are a single fixed instrument
distractors.why: there are thousands of variants tuned for tax/balance-sheet/regulatory needs

nodes.sample_question: Why is preference share capital described as a hybrid instrument? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Classifying preference/convertible instruments as pure debt or pure equity.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Equity is RISK capital (participates in the venture's risk), PATIENT capital (willing to wait years for a return — e.g. a drug takes 12-15 years), and PERMANENT capital (stays on the books unless bought back — buybacks are uncommon), giving the enterprise financial STABILITY (no compulsory dividends/repayment). Equity holders earn returns two ways: periodic DIVIDENDS (paid out of profit after tax, but DISCRETIONARY — the board may retain earnings) and CAPITAL APPRECIATION (share value rising). Neither is guaranteed.

distractors.wrong: Equity holders are guaranteed dividends
distractors.why: dividends are discretionary (board decides); the only guaranteed feature is participation in risk/reward

distractors.wrong: Equity capital must be repaid on a schedule like a loan
distractors.why: equity is permanent/patient capital — it stays on the books, bringing financial stability

nodes.sample_question: What does it mean that equity is 'risk', 'patient' and 'permanent' capital, and what are its two return sources? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Expecting guaranteed dividends or scheduled repayment from equity.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Equity is not a 'free lunch'. Raising it means: (1) giving away OWNERSHIP and a share of WEALTH (dilution); (2) granting VOTING RIGHTS — every share carries one vote, so shareholders gain a say in management; (3) GOVERNANCE OBLIGATIONS — shareholder rights and board duties are enshrined in the Companies Act 2013; and (4) LUMPINESS — unlike loans (any size), share capital is hard to raise in tiny amounts and comes in lumps. So equity shares two things: wealth and control.

distractors.wrong: Equity is cheaper than debt because it has no interest cost
distractors.why: equity costs ownership, wealth-share, control and governance obligations — not free

distractors.wrong: Share capital can be raised in any small amount like a loan
distractors.why: share capital is LUMPY — hard to raise tiny sums; it comes in lumps

nodes.sample_question: What are the downsides of raising equity share capital? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating equity as a costless source and ignoring control/governance/lumpiness.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.formula: ownership_% = shares_held / total_shares; voting_% = ownership_%; wealth_share = ownership_% x sale_value
nodes.teaching_note: Equity bundles two rights: CASH-FLOW (wealth) rights and CONTROL (voting) rights, each proportional to %shareholding. Illustration: a Rs 10,000 kirana company issues 1,000 shares of Rs 10 each; X subscribes 600 (Rs 6,000), Y subscribes 400 (Rs 4,000) -> ownership 60:40. Each share = one vote, so X controls 60%, Y 40%. If later sold for Rs 1 lakh, X gets Rs 60,000 and Y Rs 40,000 (wealth split in the same ratio). By taking Rs 4,000 from Y, X gave up 40% of both wealth and control.

distractors.wrong: Voting rights can differ from %equity for ordinary shares
distractors.why: ordinary shares carry one vote each, so voting % equals equity % (60:40 here)

distractors.wrong: Wealth and control rights are split differently
distractors.why: both cash-flow (wealth) and control (voting) rights track the same %shareholding

nodes.sample_question: X subscribes 600 shares and Y 400 shares of a 1,000-share company at Rs 10 each. State each holder's ownership %, voting %, and share of a Rs 1 lakh sale. (calculation)
nodes.failure_mode: Separating wealth from control rights when ordinary shares bundle them in the same ratio.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Four levels of share capital (descending): AUTHORISED capital (maximum the company may issue, set in the Memorandum; can be raised by amending the MOA) >= ISSUED capital (shares offered for subscription) >= SUBSCRIBED capital (shares investors agree to take) >= PAID-UP / called-up capital (money actually called/paid). FACE VALUE is the nominal value per share (any multiple of Re 1 under Indian law, e.g. Rs 10); it has limited financial significance. Money paid ABOVE face value goes to the securities-premium account.

distractors.wrong: Authorised and paid-up capital are the same
distractors.why: authorised is the MAXIMUM permitted; paid-up is the amount actually paid in — paid-up <= subscribed <= issued <= authorised

distractors.wrong: Face value is the market value of a share
distractors.why: face value is the nominal value (e.g. Rs 10); premium above it goes to securities premium

nodes.sample_question: Define authorised, issued, subscribed and paid-up capital and order them. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing authorised (a ceiling) with paid-up (actual), or face value with market price.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.concept: Net worth, book value & market cap
nodes.formula: net_worth = share_capital + reserves_surplus; book_value_per_share = net_worth / shares_outstanding; market_cap = price x shares
nodes.teaching_note: NET WORTH (book equity) = equity share capital + reserves & surplus (accumulated retained profits). BOOK VALUE PER SHARE = net worth / number of shares outstanding. MARKET CAPITALISATION = market price per share x number of shares (the market value of equity). Dividend % is expressed on FACE VALUE (a 10% dividend on a Rs 10 face value = Re 1/share). Example: net worth Rs 15,00,000 over 10,000 shares -> book value Rs 150/share.

distractors.wrong: Book value per share equals the face value
distractors.why: book value per share = net worth/shares (includes reserves); face value is just the nominal value

distractors.wrong: Net worth is only the share capital
distractors.why: net worth = share capital PLUS reserves & surplus (retained profits)

nodes.sample_question: A company has net worth of Rs 15,00,000 and 10,000 shares outstanding. Compute book value per share. (calculation)
nodes.failure_mode: Omitting reserves & surplus from net worth, or confusing book value with face/market value.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Equity is raised in STAGES reflecting falling risk as the venture proves itself. The ladder: (1) the 3 Fs (founders, family, friends) at idea/proof-of-concept; (2) DEVELOPMENT AGENCIES / government grants (for science-intensive sectors where markets are thin); (3) ANGELS, INCUBATORS and ACCELERATORS; (4) VENTURE CAPITAL / private equity (institutional); (5) the PUBLIC EQUITY market (IPO) — which also creates a mechanism for early investors to exit. The sequence is market practice, not law.

distractors.wrong: Start-ups must follow a fixed legally-mandated funding sequence
distractors.why: the sequence is market practice, not law; companies can skip stages

distractors.wrong: Government/development agencies invest for profit
distractors.why: they provide risk capital/grants for economic-development goals, not primarily profit

nodes.sample_question: List the sources of equity capital in the typical order a start-up taps them. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating the funding ladder as a legal requirement rather than market practice.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: The first external capital is the 3 Fs — founders, family and friends. Their funding is NOT arm's-length: motivation is to SUPPORT the entrepreneur (and 'psychic income' from success), not commercial return. Consequences: they are unlikely to threaten control or impose management DISCIPLINE, may lack the background to add value, and may not understand that equity can't simply be returned on demand. As many small holders accumulate, managing the share-capital base/cap table becomes a problem.

distractors.wrong: 3F money is arm's-length, return-motivated capital
distractors.why: 3Fs invest to support the founder (psychic income), not for commercial return

distractors.wrong: 3F investors bring management discipline like VCs
distractors.why: they rarely impose discipline or covenants; their value-add is limited

nodes.sample_question: How does 3F (founders/family/friends) capital differ from arm's-length investment? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Expecting 3Fs to behave like return-driven institutional investors.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: ANGELS are high-net-worth individuals investing their own money for RETURN (arm's-length, unlike 3Fs), typically Rs 20 lakh to Rs 4-5 cr, often with mentorship. ANGEL NETWORKS pool many angels: benefits are (1) spreading capital across more investments (lower risk per deal), (2) a shared SECRETARIAT for sourcing/initial due diligence (cost distributed), and (3) access to a larger pool of EXPERTISE. Crucially, each angel retains DISCRETION on which deals to join (unlike a VC fund where the fund manager decides). Membership fee ~Rs 1 lakh/year. Examples: Indian Angel Network, Chennai/Mumbai Angel Networks.

distractors.wrong: In an angel network the manager decides each member's investments
distractors.why: each angel retains DISCRETION on which deals to join — unlike a VC fund where the manager decides

distractors.wrong: Angels and the 3 Fs share the same motivation
distractors.why: angels are arm's-length, return-motivated; 3Fs invest to support the founder

nodes.sample_question: What benefits does an angel network give over investing as an individual angel? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing angel-network discretion with VC-fund discretionary decision-making.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: INCUBATORS help convert a raw idea into an enterprise by providing resources start-ups lack — lab/pilot-plant facilities, mentors, manufacturing and managerial talent, and small seed funding — motivated by development plus a hope of equity upside. Most academic institutions (IISc, IITs) run incubators. ACCELERATORS are a related but distinct cohort-based model (the best-known is Y Combinator in the US, which has accelerated 500+ start-ups). Both fill resource gaps (capital + management talent) at an early stage.

distractors.wrong: Incubators and accelerators are the same institution
distractors.why: they are related but distinct; accelerators run fixed cohorts (e.g. Y Combinator)

distractors.wrong: Incubators only provide cash
distractors.why: they provide lab/pilot facilities, mentors, manufacturing and managerial talent plus small seed funding

nodes.sample_question: Distinguish an incubator from an accelerator, with an example of each. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Conflating incubators (resource providers) with cohort-based accelerators.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: VENTURE CAPITAL is the institutional source after angels/networks (sequence is market practice, not law). The PUBLIC EQUITY market (stock exchange) is the last source: it lets companies raise large sums and lets early investors SELL/exit. Access is restricted by SEBI regulations and stock-exchange listing criteria — only companies that meet quality/profitability/balance-sheet thresholds may list — to PROTECT retail investors from irresponsible promoters. The downside: many genuine start-ups don't yet qualify, so public markets aren't available to all.

distractors.wrong: Any company can raise money on the public market at will
distractors.why: SEBI/exchange listing criteria restrict access to protect retail investors; many start-ups don't qualify

distractors.wrong: VC always comes after angel funding
distractors.why: the sequence is market practice; some companies go to VC without prior angel rounds

nodes.sample_question: Why is access to the public equity market restricted, and who enforces it? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming public markets are open to all start-ups, or that the funding sequence is legally fixed.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: What different investors want falls into four buckets: (1) RETURNS (dividends + capital appreciation); (2) LIQUIDITY (ability to convert the investment back into cash); (3) STRATEGIC benefits (e.g. Cisco/Intel acquiring/driving demand for their products); (4) PSYCHIC income (psychological satisfaction). Matching: 3Fs seek psychic income; angels seek returns + engagement; VCs seek return + liquidity; strategic investors seek strategic benefits (with restrictive terms to scrutinise); public investors seek returns and exert price pressure when disappointed.

distractors.wrong: All investors are motivated purely by financial return
distractors.why: motivations also include liquidity, strategic benefits and psychic income

distractors.wrong: Strategic investors mainly want financial return
distractors.why: strategic investors (Cisco/Intel) seek strategic benefits, often with restrictive terms

nodes.sample_question: Name the four buckets of investor motivation and match a source to each. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Reducing all investors to return-seekers and missing liquidity/strategic/psychic motives.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: The VC process is a funnel: SOURCING (examine many deals — roughly 1 investment per 100-1,000 plans, per a 2019 HBS survey) -> SCREENING (reject 80-90% quickly against sector/stage/geography criteria) -> EVALUATION/due diligence (founder background, industry, business model, valuation) -> TERM SHEET (preliminary expression of interest) -> due diligence on books/contracts -> final VALUATION -> CONTRACTING/documentation (shareholders'/share-purchase/investment agreements, money transferred) -> post-investment engagement -> EXIT (~4-5 years). The standard sequence: Sourcing -> Screening -> Evaluation -> Structuring -> Contracting -> Exit.

distractors.wrong: The investment sequence is Sourcing -> Structuring -> Screening -> Evaluation
distractors.why: the correct order is Sourcing -> Screening -> Evaluation -> Structuring -> Contracting -> Exit

distractors.wrong: VCs invest in most deals they see
distractors.why: they invest in roughly 1 of 100-1,000; the vast majority are screened out quickly

nodes.sample_question: State the correct sequence of stages in the VC investment process. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Mis-ordering the process (e.g. structuring before screening/evaluation).

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Founders should be ready to answer what VCs look for: (1) what PROBLEM/pain point is solved and the customer BENEFIT (not feature specs — a common founder mistake); (2) is the problem IMPORTANT enough (market SIZE — TAM/SAM/SOM); (3) is someone already meeting the need (COMPETITION) and what is your DEFENSIBILITY (product, lock-in, pricing — e.g. OYO vs Stayzilla); (4) delivered COST vs PRICE and sustainable margin (unit economics); (5) how much money is needed; (6) the EXIT for the investor (when/how/how much more); (7) is this the best TEAM to execute. VCs seek wealth multiplication via large markets and rapid growth.

distractors.wrong: Founders should pitch product features/specifications
distractors.why: pitch the customer BENEFIT, not features — emphasising specs is a common mistake

distractors.wrong: First-mover advantage means competition can be ignored
distractors.why: incumbents/imitators can take share (OYO vs Stayzilla); defensibility must be shown

nodes.sample_question: What does a VC look for in a founder's pitch (investment criteria)? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Pitching features over benefits, or ignoring competition/defensibility and the exit.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Zomato's pre-IPO prospectus shows ~17 funding ROUNDS raising ~Rs 112 bn (~$2.5 bn) from ~20 lead institutional investors (out of ~90-100 total shareholders, including early angels). Lessons: large high-growth start-ups raise repeatedly; early rounds are small and frequent (burning cash to grow), later rounds larger with longer gaps; staying PRIVATE for ~10 years enabled easy PIVOTS (a strategy change with the same vision); SECONDARY purchases (later investors buying out earlier ones, e.g. Tiger/Accel) gave early investors liquidity while the company stayed private; investors form syndicates/consortia (lead + smaller roles).

distractors.wrong: Zomato raised in a few large rounds
distractors.why: it raised ~17 rounds — small/frequent early, larger/spaced later

distractors.wrong: Early investors must wait for IPO to get liquidity
distractors.why: SECONDARY purchases let earlier investors exit to later investors while the company stays private

nodes.sample_question: What does Zomato's funding history illustrate about how high-growth start-ups raise capital? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Missing the role of secondaries and staying-private-for-pivots in a long funding journey.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: EVOLVED firms have long operating histories with STABILISED operating economics (stable sales-cost relationships), audited/regulated data and an actively-traded share price — so DCF and historical comparison work well. EARLY-STAGE firms lack this; their valuation is heavily influenced by the AVAILABILITY of capital and INVESTOR PREFERENCE for the sector (a hot sector, e.g. AI, inflates valuations like demand inflating the price of oranges/gold). So early-stage valuation is as much about market conditions as fundamentals.

distractors.wrong: Early-stage firms are valued like evolved firms using DCF on history
distractors.why: early-stage firms lack stable history; valuation hinges on capital availability and investor sector-preference

distractors.wrong: Investor preference for a sector doesn't affect valuation
distractors.why: capital chasing a hot sector (e.g. AI) inflates valuations regardless of fundamentals

nodes.sample_question: Why is valuing an early-stage firm different from valuing an evolved firm? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Applying stable-history DCF logic to an early-stage firm whose value is sentiment/capital-driven.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Three valuation approaches: (1) DISCOUNTED CASH FLOW (DCF) — forecast sales/profits/cash flows and discount them (suits firms with forecastable history); (2) PRICE-TO-EARNINGS (P/E) — current price relative to earnings per share; (3) PRICE-TO-BOOK (P/B) — current price relative to book value per share. For loss-making firms (no PAT) the EV/EBITDA multiple is used instead of P/E. P/E, P/B and EV/EBITDA are 'accounting comparables' methods relying on the principle that similar firms command similar multiples.

distractors.wrong: DCF is the only valuation method
distractors.why: DCF, P/E, P/B and EV/EBITDA are all used; the right one depends on the firm's data

distractors.wrong: P/E works for loss-making firms
distractors.why: with no profit after tax, P/E is meaningless; use EV/EBITDA instead

nodes.sample_question: Name the main valuation methods and when EV/EBITDA is used instead of P/E. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Applying P/E to a pre-profit firm instead of EV/EBITDA.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.formula: P/E = price / EPS; EPS = PAT / shares; P/B = price / BVPS; BVPS = net_worth / shares

variables.BVPS: book value per share = net worth/shares

nodes.teaching_note: P/E ratio = market price per share / earnings per share (EPS = PAT/shares). P/B ratio = market price per share / book value per share (BVPS = net worth/shares). The key insight: within an INDUSTRY, firms have SIMILAR P/E and P/B ratios (they are industry characteristics reflecting the industry's capital-to-profit and investment-to-sales relationships). A P/B BELOW 1 may indicate the company is UNDERVALUED. Worked example: price Rs 200; 10,000 shares of Rs 100 face value (= Rs 10,00,000 capital) + Rs 5,00,000 retained earnings -> net worth Rs 15,00,000 -> BVPS Rs 150 -> P/B = 200/150 = 1.33.

distractors.wrong: P/E and P/B vary randomly across firms in an industry
distractors.why: they are INDUSTRY characteristics — similar firms in the same industry have similar ratios

distractors.wrong: A P/B below 1 means the firm is overvalued
distractors.why: P/B < 1 may indicate the firm is UNDERvalued (price below book value)

nodes.sample_question: A share trades at Rs 200; the firm has 10,000 shares of Rs 100 face value and Rs 5,00,000 retained earnings. Compute the P/B ratio. (calculation)
nodes.failure_mode: Using face value instead of book value per share, or omitting retained earnings from net worth.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.formula: EV = equity_market_value + debt - cash; equity_value = EV - debt - preference

variables.EBITDA: earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, amortisation

nodes.teaching_note: For firms with little/no profit after tax (Zomato, Paytm, Delhivery at IPO), use EV/EBITDA instead of P/E. EBITDA = earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, amortisation. ENTERPRISE VALUE (EV) = market value of equity + debt - cash. EV/EBITDA is even more of an industry characteristic than P/E because it is INDEPENDENT of capital structure (it sits above interest/depreciation, which differ with borrowing policy). To get equity value back from EV: equity value = EV - debt (- preference). Worked example: equity Rs 800 cr + debt Rs 300 cr - cash Rs 100 cr = EV Rs 1,000 cr.

distractors.wrong: Enterprise value equals the market value of equity
distractors.why: EV = equity + debt - cash; it is the value of the whole firm, not just equity

distractors.wrong: EV/EBITDA depends on capital structure like P/E
distractors.why: EV/EBITDA is independent of capital structure (above interest/depreciation), so it's more comparable across firms

nodes.sample_question: A firm has equity market value Rs 800 cr, debt Rs 300 cr and cash Rs 100 cr. Compute enterprise value. (calculation)
nodes.failure_mode: Forgetting to add debt and subtract cash, or confusing EV with equity value.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: To value a target firm T by comparables: (1) IDENTIFY similar firms (same industry/products/customers) — listed firms (calc ratios directly) or recent comparable TRANSACTIONS; (2) CALCULATE their average P/E (or EV/EBITDA, EV/sales); (3) ESTIMATE the target's metric (forecast EPS_T, or EBITDA, or sales); (4) MULTIPLY: justified price = EPS_T x industry-average P/E. The principle is the 'Parker-pen' logic: value is relative to comparable products. P/E suits profitable, comparable firms; it is unsuitable for loss-making firms or where growth prospects differ widely (use EV/EBITDA or EV/sales).

distractors.wrong: Any set of firms can be compared using P/E
distractors.why: P/E comparison fails for loss-making firms or firms with very different growth prospects — use EV/EBITDA

distractors.wrong: You can value a firm from its own numbers alone
distractors.why: comparables value is relative — you need similar listed firms or comparable transactions

nodes.sample_question: List the steps of the P/E comparables method to value a target firm. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Applying P/E to non-comparable or loss-making firms instead of EV/EBITDA or EV/sales.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Unit economics asks: per unit sold, does revenue exceed the cost to make/deliver/acquire? A positive contribution margin = strong unit economics; spending Rs 600 to earn Rs 500 per customer = NEGATIVE unit economics. CONTRIBUTION MARGIN = (price - variable/raw-material cost)/price. CUSTOMER LIFETIME VALUE (CLV) = (revenue per period x contribution-margin %)/CHURN rate; compare to customer ACQUISITION COST (CAC) via the CLV/CAC ratio (a healthy ratio is well above 1). Luckin Coffee example: high contribution margin but promotions and churn threaten store-level profitability while per-customer CLV/CAC stays healthy.

distractors.wrong: Strong unit economics just means high revenue
distractors.why: it means revenue per unit exceeds the cost to make/deliver/acquire it (positive contribution margin)

distractors.wrong: CLV ignores churn
distractors.why: CLV = (revenue x contribution margin)/churn; higher churn lowers CLV

nodes.sample_question: A firm earns Rs 500 revenue per customer and spends Rs 600 to acquire and serve them. What does this indicate about unit economics? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Equating unit economics with revenue scale rather than per-unit margin vs cost.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.formula: new_% = old_% x (1 - dilution_fraction); absolute_shares unchanged in a primary round

variables.dilution_fraction: % of equity issued to the new investor

nodes.teaching_note: Dilution = the fall in an existing holder's OWNERSHIP % when the company issues NEW shares to a new investor. The company prints new shares (not the founder selling theirs — the company, not the founder, needs the money). Key facts: existing holders' ABSOLUTE share count stays the same; only their PERCENTAGE drops. New % = old % x (1 - dilution fraction). Dilution can be GOOD: if the round raises value, the founder's smaller % can be worth more in money. Example: founder 800 shares; issue 200 to an investor -> 1,000 total -> founder 80% (diluted 20%, but still owns 800 shares). A second 250-share round -> founder 64% (= 80% x (1-0.2)).

distractors.wrong: Dilution reduces the founder's absolute number of shares
distractors.why: absolute shares stay constant in a pure primary round; only the PERCENTAGE falls

distractors.wrong: Dilution always makes the founder poorer
distractors.why: if the round raises value, a smaller % can be worth more money than the larger % before

nodes.sample_question: A founder owns 800 shares; the company issues 200 new shares to an investor. What is the founder's ownership % and how many shares do they still own? (calculation)
nodes.failure_mode: Thinking dilution cuts the founder's share count, or that dilution is always value-destroying.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.formula: post_money = investment / equity_%; pre_money = post_money - investment; equity_% = investment / (pre_money + investment)
nodes.teaching_note: POST-MONEY valuation = investment / %equity given for it. PRE-MONEY valuation = post-money - investment. Pre-money = the notional value of the company's OTHER assets (founder's IP/idea) before the new cash. Post-money INCLUDES the incoming investment; pre-money EXCLUDES it. Worked examples (CLA-verified): invest Rs 25 cr for 25% -> post = 25/0.25 = Rs 100 cr; pre-money Rs 60 cr + raise Rs 15 cr -> investor % = 15/(60+15) = 20%; invest Rs 8 M for 25% -> post = Rs 32 M; pre Rs 40 M + raise Rs 10 M -> investor % = 10/50 = 20%.

distractors.wrong: Pre-money valuation includes the incoming investment
distractors.why: PRE-money EXCLUDES it; POST-money = pre-money + investment

distractors.wrong: %stake = investment / pre-money valuation
distractors.why: %stake = investment / POST-money (= pre + investment); using pre-money overstates the stake

nodes.sample_question: A start-up has a pre-money valuation of Rs 60 cr and raises Rs 15 cr. What % stake does the investor get? (calculation)
nodes.failure_mode: Dividing by pre-money instead of post-money, or swapping pre and post.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.formula: equity_%_at_exit = required_realisation / exit_valuation; required_realisation = investment x target_multiple

variables.exit_valuation: forecast value of whole equity at exit

nodes.teaching_note: To find the % of the WHOLE company an investor must own at EXIT to hit their return: %equity at exit = investor's required cash realisation / exit valuation of the enterprise. Exit valuation is often a multiple of forecast sales (EV/sales) or EBITDA. Kloud Garage example: exit valuation = 5 x year-5 sales (Rs 1,200 M) = Rs 6,000 M; round-1 investor needs 16 x Rs 130 M = Rs 2,080 M -> %equity at exit = 2,080/6,000 = 34.7%.

distractors.wrong: %equity at exit = investment / exit valuation
distractors.why: it is the required REALISATION (= investment x multiple) / exit valuation, not the raw investment

distractors.wrong: Exit valuation equals the latest funding valuation
distractors.why: exit valuation is forecast (e.g. a sales/EBITDA multiple of a future year), not the entry valuation

nodes.sample_question: An investor must realise Rs 2,080 M and the firm's exit valuation is Rs 6,000 M. What % equity must they hold at exit? (calculation)
nodes.failure_mode: Using raw investment instead of required realisation, or confusing exit with entry valuation.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.formula: entry_% = exit_% / (1 - next_round_dilution); cap table sums to 100%

variables.next_round_dilution: fraction of equity the later round takes

nodes.teaching_note: An early investor's % at EXIT is lower than at ENTRY because later rounds dilute them. To find the ENTRY % needed to end up with a target exit %, REVERSE the dilution: entry % = exit % / (1 - later-round dilution). Kloud Garage: round-1 investor must hold 34.7% at exit; round 2 takes 35%, so round-1 entry % = 34.7/(1-0.35) = 53.3%; founder after round 1 = 100 - 53.3 = 46.7%. The final CAP TABLE must sum to 100% (founder 30.3% + round-1 34.7% + round-2 35% = 100%).

distractors.wrong: Entry % equals exit % (dilution is ignored)
distractors.why: later rounds dilute the early investor, so entry % = exit % / (1 - later dilution) > exit %

distractors.wrong: The cap table need not sum to 100%
distractors.why: all stakeholders' percentages must sum to exactly 100% (within rounding)

nodes.sample_question: A round-1 investor must hold 34.7% at exit; a later round takes 35%. What entry % must round 1 have acquired? (calculation)
nodes.failure_mode: Forgetting to gross up the entry stake for later-round dilution, or a cap table that doesn't sum to 100%.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.formula: required_stake = investment x (1+r)^n / exit_equity_value; annual_return = multiple^(1/n) - 1
nodes.teaching_note: To find the %stake an investor should seek so a target ANNUAL return is met over n years (no further dilution): required %stake = future value of investment / exit equity value, where future value = investment x (1 + r)^n (time value of money). CLA-verified example: invest Rs 10 cr at 30% p.a. for 5 years -> FV = 10 x 1.3^5 = Rs 37.13 cr; if exit equity value = Rs 186 cr, required stake = 37.13/186 = ~20%. (A money MULTIPLE m over n years implies annual return r = m^(1/n) - 1; e.g. 16x over 4 years = 16^0.25 - 1 = 100% p.a.)

distractors.wrong: Required stake = investment / exit value (ignoring compounding)
distractors.why: the investment must grow at the target return: use FV = investment x (1+r)^n in the numerator

distractors.wrong: A 16x multiple over 4 years is a 16% annual return
distractors.why: annual return = 16^(1/4) - 1 = 100% p.a.; multiples and annual rates are not the same

nodes.sample_question: An investor puts in Rs 10 cr expecting 30% p.a. for 5 years; exit equity value is Rs 186 cr. What %stake should they seek (no dilution)? (calculation)
nodes.failure_mode: Skipping the (1+r)^n compounding, or equating a money multiple with an annual return.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.formula: multiple = (equity_%_at_exit x exit_valuation) / investment; annual_return = multiple^(1/n) - 1
nodes.teaching_note: The exit MULTIPLE = investor's realisation / investment = (%stake x exit valuation) / investment. CLA-verified example: invest Rs 20 cr for 25%, company exits at Rs 200 cr (no further dilution) -> realisation = 0.25 x 200 = Rs 50 cr -> multiple = 50/20 = 2.5x. The implied annual return (CAGR/IRR analogue) = multiple^(1/n) - 1. Investors usually state expectations as multiples; translate to % to compare (e.g. 16x over 4 years = 100% p.a.).

distractors.wrong: Exit multiple = exit valuation / investment
distractors.why: it is the investor's REALISATION (= %stake x exit valuation) / investment, not the whole exit valuation

distractors.wrong: A higher multiple over more years is always a higher annual return
distractors.why: annual return = multiple^(1/n) - 1; a big multiple over many years can be a modest annual rate

nodes.sample_question: An investor holds 25% and the company exits at Rs 200 cr on a Rs 20 cr investment. What is the exit multiple? (calculation)
nodes.failure_mode: Dividing exit valuation (not the investor's realisation) by the investment, or ignoring the holding period.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Pulling the cap-table maths together, valuing a start-up runs: (1) estimate FUNDING REQUIREMENT (CapEx + operational cash burn/deficits); (2) funding TIMELINE; (3) plan TRANCHES/rounds; (4) the investor MULTIPLE expected; (5) expected YEAR of exit; (6) HOLDING PERIOD per round; (7) EXIT VALUATION of the enterprise (sales/EBITDA multiple); (8) %equity at exit (= realisation/exit valuation); (9) ADJUST for dilution to get %equity at ENTRY; (10) compute POST- and PRE-money valuation. Each step rests on assumptions; the model is a planning/negotiation tool, not gospel.

distractors.wrong: Valuation is a single calculation
distractors.why: it is a chain of ~10 steps from funding requirement through exit valuation to pre/post money

distractors.wrong: The funding requirement is only capital expenditure
distractors.why: it is CapEx PLUS operational cash burn/deficits

nodes.sample_question: Outline the steps to value a start-up from funding requirement to pre/post-money valuation. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Skipping the dilution adjustment or the cash-burn component of the funding requirement.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Pre- and post-money valuations RISING from round to round SIGNAL progress: an arm's-length investor paying a higher valuation in a later round VALIDATES the founder and confirms the company's development (product built, traction). It also raises the value of EARLIER investors' stakes. Pre-money valuation is the notional value of the company's non-cash assets at the time of a round; the trend line across rounds is the key signal that later investors and founders watch.

distractors.wrong: Rising valuations across rounds are meaningless noise
distractors.why: they signal validated progress — an arm's-length higher valuation confirms development and lifts earlier stakes

distractors.wrong: Only the latest investor benefits from a higher round
distractors.why: earlier investors' stakes also rise in value when a later round prices the company higher

nodes.sample_question: What does a rising pre/post-money valuation across rounds signal? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Ignoring valuation trend as a signal of validated progress.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Convertibles let an investor PROTECT against the DOWNSIDE (price/valuation risk). If a founder is over-optimistic and the exit valuation falls (e.g. year-4 sales Rs 800 M not Rs 1,200 M -> exit valuation Rs 4,000 M not Rs 6,000 M), an investor locked into equity at a fixed price gets less. Instead, the investor funds via a CONVERTIBLE instrument (convertible preference share / loan / debenture) that converts at a price based on ACTUAL performance -> buys more shares at a lower average price if the firm underperforms. It is also fair to the founder (an incentive to deliver). Outcome depends on bargaining power.

distractors.wrong: Convertibles only benefit the founder
distractors.why: they primarily protect the INVESTOR against downside price/valuation risk, while also incentivising the founder

distractors.wrong: An investor locked into equity at a fixed price is protected if valuation falls
distractors.why: a fixed-price equity holder LOSES if valuation falls; convertibles let them re-price to actual performance

nodes.sample_question: How does funding via a convertible instrument protect an investor against valuation risk? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Thinking a fixed-price equity stake protects against a falling exit valuation.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: A valuation model rests on many UNREALISTIC assumptions, so use it as a PLANNING and NEGOTIATION tool, not gospel truth. Its value is forcing disciplined thinking (funding requirement, timeline, return, exit) and enabling SCENARIO analysis. Kloud Garage scenario: raising LESS upfront (Rs 70 M + Rs 480 M instead of Rs 130 M + Rs 420 M) lowers entry equity to 31.1% from 53.3% -> less founder dilution, because raising large sums early (held longer, higher uncertainty) demands higher returns and lower valuations.

distractors.wrong: The valuation model gives the true value of the company
distractors.why: it rests on unrealistic assumptions; it's a planning/negotiation tool, not truth

distractors.wrong: Raising more money upfront is always better
distractors.why: raising more upfront increases dilution (longer hold, higher uncertainty, lower valuation); staging can reduce it

nodes.sample_question: Why should a start-up valuation model be treated as a planning tool rather than the truth? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating model outputs as precise truth, or assuming more upfront funding is costless.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Financial planning for a start-up runs: SALES estimate -> UNIT COSTS & operating-expense forecast -> CASH BUDGET -> forecast FINANCIAL STATEMENTS (P&L, balance sheet, cash flow) -> FUNDING plan -> VALUATION. A financial FORECAST projects revenues, expenses and cash flows (NOT just historical statements; weather/office location/employee names are irrelevant). In early-stage firms the business STORY and the finance are intimately connected, unlike mature firms.

distractors.wrong: A financial forecast is just historical financial statements
distractors.why: a forecast PROJECTS future revenues, expenses and cash flows; history alone isn't a forecast

distractors.wrong: Cash budgeting comes before estimating sales
distractors.why: planning starts with the SALES estimate, then costs, then the cash budget

nodes.sample_question: What are the steps of financial planning for a start-up, and what does a financial forecast contain? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Mis-ordering planning steps or thinking a forecast is just past statements.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: A CASH BUDGET is a statement of RECEIPTS and PAYMENTS over each period (a month for volatile start-ups), like a household budget, focused on the CLOSING CASH BALANCE. Receipts - payments = surplus (if receipts > payments) or deficit. Its most direct purpose is to ESTIMATE the FUNDING REQUIREMENT over the planning horizon. Start-ups typically have cash OUT before cash IN (free trials, no early revenue), so cumulative deficits build up before turning positive.

distractors.wrong: A cash budget's main purpose is to segment customers or plan staffing
distractors.why: its most direct purpose is to ESTIMATE the funding requirement over the planning horizon

distractors.wrong: A cash budget is the same as a profit & loss account
distractors.why: it tracks cash receipts/payments and the closing cash balance, not accrual profit

nodes.sample_question: What is a cash budget and what does it most directly enable a start-up to estimate? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing the cash budget (cash) with the P&L (accrual), or missing its funding-estimate purpose.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.formula: net_cash_burn = cash_payments - cash_receipts; runway = cash_balance / monthly_burn
nodes.teaching_note: When a start-up's PAYMENTS exceed its RECEIPTS it is BURNING cash. NET CASH BURN = cash payments - cash receipts (for the period). A HIGH burn rate means the company is spending cash rapidly (not that it is profitable or generating surplus). RUNWAY = cash balance / monthly burn = how long before cash runs out. 'Cash, cash, cash' is the start-up mantra — running out of cash (e.g. unable to pay salaries) can fold the company. CLA-verified: receipts Rs 2,00,000, payments Rs 5,00,000 -> net burn Rs 3,00,000.

distractors.wrong: A high burn rate indicates high profitability
distractors.why: high burn means cash is being spent rapidly, NOT that the firm is profitable

distractors.wrong: Net burn = total payments
distractors.why: net burn = payments MINUS receipts; receipts offset some of the spend

nodes.sample_question: A start-up has monthly receipts of Rs 2,00,000 and payments of Rs 5,00,000. What is the net cash burn? (calculation)
nodes.failure_mode: Equating burn with total spend (ignoring receipts) or reading high burn as profitability.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: TOTAL FUNDING REQUIREMENT = PEAK cumulative OPERATIONAL cash deficit + INVESTMENT (CapEx: infrastructure + technology). The operational cash deficit is the cumulative (receipts - payments) before the business turns cash-positive; holding the peak deficit as a cash buffer ensures you never run out while building (e.g. ~15-16 months for a Kareer Sciences centre). For multi-unit businesses, multiply per-unit peak deficit and per-unit CapEx by the number of units, then add any shared technology investment.

distractors.wrong: Funding requirement is just the capital expenditure
distractors.why: it is CapEx PLUS the peak cumulative operational cash deficit (the cash burn buffer)

distractors.wrong: You only need the deficit of the worst single month
distractors.why: you need the PEAK CUMULATIVE deficit, which builds up over many months

nodes.sample_question: How is a start-up's total funding requirement calculated from its cash budget? (calculation)
nodes.failure_mode: Omitting the operational cash-deficit buffer or using a single-month rather than cumulative peak.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Cash-budget line items split into RECURRING (P&L) items — revenue (clients x fee), cost of associates (headcount x salary), overheads (often ~100% of associate cost), marketing costs — and ONE-TIME (balance-sheet/CapEx) items — infrastructure investment and technology investment. In the cash budget you record each as a RECEIPT or PAYMENT in the month it hits cash. Kareer Sciences ratios: associate handles 10 clients (160 hrs / 16 hrs per client); associates needed = clients/10; fee Rs 25,000/client; max 15 associates per 150-client centre.

distractors.wrong: All cash-budget items are recurring operating expenses
distractors.why: infrastructure and technology are ONE-TIME CapEx, distinct from recurring salary/overhead/marketing

distractors.wrong: The cash budget records accrual revenue and expense
distractors.why: it records cash RECEIPTS and PAYMENTS in the month they hit cash

nodes.sample_question: Distinguish the recurring (P&L) from the one-time (CapEx) line items in a start-up cash budget. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Mixing CapEx with recurring costs, or recording accruals instead of cash flows.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: In a start-up, GROWTH STRATEGY, capital requirement and DILUTION are intimately linked (unlike mature firms). Faster growth needs more capital and (if raised upfront) causes more dilution. Kareer Sciences 'lazy/cozy/crazy' paths (1-2-4 / 4-8-12 / 12-24-36 centres) need rising capital (lazy ~Rs 155 lakh; cozy ~Rs 465 lakh; crazy + ~Rs 10 cr software) and imply higher exit %equity given to investors (38.9% / 31.4% / 61%) because faster growth = higher perceived risk = higher demanded multiple = more dilution. Raising upfront gives certainty but at lower valuation/higher dilution; staging (defer the Rs 10 cr software raise) earns a better valuation once de-risked.

distractors.wrong: Faster growth strategies reduce the capital a start-up needs
distractors.why: faster growth needs MORE capital and (if raised upfront) causes MORE dilution

distractors.wrong: Raising all funds upfront minimises dilution
distractors.why: upfront raises occur at lower valuation/higher dilution; staging after de-risking improves valuation

nodes.sample_question: How are a start-up's growth strategy, capital requirement and founder dilution linked? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming faster growth is capital-light or that upfront raising minimises dilution.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Kareer Sciences (fictional) is a career-counselling start-up built on the 3E model (Endowments, Education, Environment) with four components (networked mentoring, deep psychometric evaluation, demand-side data, an opportunity repository), measured by fit/satisfaction/longevity/financial outcomes. It is modelled as an agglomeration of identical 'centres' to illustrate the cash budget and the link between growth path and valuation/dilution. Exit valuation = a sales multiple (2x lazy, 4x cozy/crazy); investor %equity rises with growth-path risk.

distractors.wrong: Kareer Sciences is valued by DCF on long history
distractors.why: as an early-stage firm it is valued by a sales multiple at exit, not DCF on history

distractors.wrong: The 3E model stands for three financial ratios
distractors.why: 3E = Endowments, Education, Environment — the drivers of career outcomes

nodes.sample_question: What is the Kareer Sciences case used to illustrate? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating the case as a real-data DCF rather than a cash-budget/growth-dilution illustration.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: STRUCTURING = designing the financing package (terms and conditions, financial and non-financial) to (a) realise the investor's RETURN objective while MITIGATING risk, and (b) leave founders/employees enough INCENTIVE (equity/upside) to make the venture succeed. It overcomes the problem of UNCERTAINTY and differing valuation expectations between founder (fears too-low valuation) and investor (fears overpaying). Good structuring ALIGNS interests so both parties become wealthy from success.

distractors.wrong: Structuring just sets the share price
distractors.why: it designs the whole package (instrument, control, incentives, protections) to align interests under uncertainty

distractors.wrong: Structuring serves only the investor
distractors.why: it must also leave founders/employees enough incentive to make the venture succeed

nodes.sample_question: What is structuring, and what two goals must it balance? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Reducing structuring to price, or ignoring founder-incentive alignment.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: In structuring, the INVESTOR wants three things: (1) rate of RETURN, (2) LIQUIDITY (ability to convert to cash — central in illiquid early-stage investing), and (3) contractual CONTROL over key decisions (because of uncertainty and the risk a founder loses interest or pursues ego over the company's best interest). The FOUNDER wants control and/or wealth — the balance varies by founder (some value control, some value wealth).

distractors.wrong: Investors care only about returns
distractors.why: they also need liquidity and contractual control — liquidity can matter as much as return

distractors.wrong: All founders prioritise control over wealth
distractors.why: founders vary: some value control (king), others wealth (rich)

nodes.sample_question: What three things does an investor seek in structuring, and what do founders seek? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Ignoring liquidity/control for investors, or assuming all founders want the same thing.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Noam Wasserman's 'Rich vs King' metaphor: a founder valuing WEALTH creation will give up CONTROL (the 'rich' path — accept dilution/investor governance to grow value); a founder valuing CONTROL will sacrifice wealth (the 'king' path — keep control, raise less, grow slower). Term-sheet conditions shape which outcome results. Neither is wrong; it depends on the founder's preference, and the choice colours every structuring decision.

distractors.wrong: The 'rich' founder keeps maximum control
distractors.why: the RICH founder gives up control to maximise wealth; the KING founder keeps control at the cost of wealth

distractors.wrong: Rich vs King is about company profitability
distractors.why: it is about the founder's trade-off between personal WEALTH and CONTROL

nodes.sample_question: Explain Wasserman's Rich vs King dilemma. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Swapping the rich (wealth, less control) and king (control, less wealth) poles.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Beyond investor/founder goals, structure is shaped by: (1) TAXATION (minimise tax for company/founder/investor — e.g. the now-repealed 'angel tax' on premiums above fair value made fundraising costly); (2) REGULATION (SEBI's Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) regulations 2012; domestic vs offshore funds; a Category I AIF must put >=75% in venture capital undertakings); (3) leaving ROOM for future investors (avoid restrictive terms — e.g. forcing the company to sell only to the investor — that deter later rounds); and (4) provision for ESOPs to incentivise key employees.

distractors.wrong: Angel tax encouraged angel investment
distractors.why: angel tax (on premiums above fair value) made fundraising costlier and was eventually repealed

distractors.wrong: Current-round terms don't affect future rounds
distractors.why: restrictive terms can make a company unattractive to later investors — leave room

nodes.sample_question: List the factors (besides investor/founder goals) that shape deal structure. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Ignoring tax/regulatory/future-investor constraints on structuring.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: A common structuring device: fund via a CONVERTIBLE instrument whose CONVERSION PRICE is LINKED to performance — better performance -> higher conversion price -> less dilution for the founder (an incentive to deliver). Performance MEASURES: profit before tax (if profitable), SALES (for pre-profit firms), MILESTONES (e.g. clinical-trial completion for a 10-12-year pharma product), or a DISCOUNT to the next round's price (e.g. convert at a 20% discount = compensation for earlier risk). The law doesn't prescribe the basis; it's an understanding between investor and founder.

distractors.wrong: Conversion price is always a fixed pre-agreed number
distractors.why: it can be linked to PBT, sales, milestones or a discount to the next round's price

distractors.wrong: Performance-linked conversion only helps the investor
distractors.why: it also incentivises the founder — better results mean a higher price and less dilution

nodes.sample_question: How can a convertible's conversion price be linked to performance, and why? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming a single fixed conversion price and missing the founder-incentive logic.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: When convertibles aren't available (regulation/preference), WARRANTS and OPTIONS achieve a similar performance-linked effect. A warrant gives the holder the RIGHT to BUY a set number of shares at a low/fixed price. The contract lets EITHER party adjust holdings by performance: if the company does BETTER than expected the FOUNDER exercises (buys cheap shares to raise their stake without much cash); if WORSE, the INVESTOR exercises (buys cheap shares to increase their stake). Considerations: tax efficiency (intrinsic-value gap may be taxable), company-law allowance, and RBI approval for cross-border (offshore-investor) cases.

distractors.wrong: Warrants always benefit the investor
distractors.why: either party can exercise: the founder if the firm outperforms, the investor if it underperforms

distractors.wrong: Warrants and convertibles are unrelated
distractors.why: warrants are a NON-convertible way to achieve the same performance-linked share adjustment

nodes.sample_question: How do warrants/options achieve performance-linked protection without a convertible? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Thinking warrants only protect the investor, or are unrelated to convertibles.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Convertibles convert into equity and come in two families: CONVERTIBLE PREFERENCE shares and CONVERTIBLE LOANS/DEBENTURES. Convertible preference is usually BETTER for the company (cleaner balance sheet; no court risk of being treated as a loan). Conversion basis: a FIXED price, a FORMULA (PBT/sales/milestones), or a DISCOUNT to the next round. OPTIONALLY convertible (the holder/company may choose to convert or redeem) vs COMPULSORILY convertible (must convert). Preference shares are CUMULATIVE (unpaid dividends carry forward) or NON-CUMULATIVE. Convertibles solve two problems: PRICE risk and LIQUIDITY risk. Offshore investors prefer convertible preference (convertible debt = cumbersome ECB).

distractors.wrong: A convertible loan is always better for the company than convertible preference
distractors.why: convertible PREFERENCE is usually better (cleaner balance sheet, no court-as-loan risk)

distractors.wrong: Compulsorily and optionally convertible are the same
distractors.why: compulsorily convertible MUST convert; optionally convertible may convert OR be redeemed

nodes.sample_question: Name the two families of convertible instruments and the difference between cumulative and non-cumulative preference shares. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing optionally vs compulsorily convertible, or cumulative vs non-cumulative dividends.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: A TERM SHEET is the investor's preliminary, NON-BINDING offer capturing the key terms (funding amount, instrument, valuation/%equity, and important conditions). It is NOT a contract — under Indian contract law a contract needs offer + acceptance + consideration; the term sheet expresses intent so both sides can negotiate without being legally locked in (a few clauses like confidentiality/exclusivity/no-shop/governing law ARE intended to bind). It is normally written BY the investor (rarely by a hot founder). Like an engagement before marriage.

distractors.wrong: A term sheet is a legally binding contract establishing ownership
distractors.why: it is primarily NON-binding (some clauses like no-shop/confidentiality bind); it expresses intent, not a contract

distractors.wrong: Founders normally write the term sheet
distractors.why: the INVESTOR normally writes it; founders writing it is rare (a very hot deal)

nodes.sample_question: What is a term sheet and is it legally binding? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating the term sheet as a binding contract, or thinking all its clauses bind.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Term-sheet length varies: angels keep them brief (2-4 pages); institutional VCs are elaborate (10-15 pages); later-stage longer. Core contents: deal details (amount, instrument, valuation/%equity), STAGING/tranches (disbursing in instalments tied to milestones), information rights, governance rights, minority protection, exit expectations, and deal-specific conditions. The NO-SHOP/exclusivity clause bars the founder from negotiating with other investors for a period (violating it by talking to another investor breaches the term sheet). Founders should want all terms surfaced EARLY, not as late surprises.

distractors.wrong: A founder who signs a term sheet may keep shopping the deal to other investors
distractors.why: the NO-SHOP clause is violated by negotiating with another investor after signing

distractors.wrong: Staging of funds is uncommon and unconditional
distractors.why: staging tied to performance milestones is common; disbursement can depend on hitting them

nodes.sample_question: A founder signs a term sheet then negotiates with another investor. Which clause is violated? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Missing the no-shop/exclusivity clause, or thinking staged disbursement is unconditional.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: INFORMATION RIGHTS let an investor MONITOR the company (not run it): business + financial reports (monthly/quarterly), audited where possible, plus inspection rights. They enable investors to track progress and intervene at the right time — they are monitoring rights, NOT management rights. BOARD rights cover composition: an investor may take a DIRECTOR seat (votes, fiduciary duty to the company) or an OBSERVER seat (attends, no vote — chosen by some foreign investors to avoid board liability), and a say in CXO appointments. Independent directors may be appointed in consultation with the investor (beneficial expertise vs nominee-alignment concern).

distractors.wrong: Information rights let investors control day-to-day operations
distractors.why: they let investors ACCESS financial information and updates to MONITOR — not run the company

distractors.wrong: A board observer can vote on resolutions
distractors.why: an observer attends but does NOT vote; only a director votes

nodes.sample_question: What are information rights for, and how does a board director seat differ from an observer seat? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating information rights as management rights, or giving an observer voting power.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: A minority investor (<50%) can't control board/shareholder votes proportionally, so investors negotiate MINORITY PROTECTION COVENANTS (a.k.a. veto rights / affirmative covenants / RESERVED MATTERS): a list of key decisions requiring the investor's POSITIVE CONSENT — issuing new shares, changing board structure, amending the AoA/MOA, borrowing above limits, selling/buying major assets, forming JVs, paying dividends, creating ESOPs, CXO appointments. Implemented via a board-meeting or shareholder-meeting veto. Reserved matters are a 'brake system': keep the list TIGHT to company-critical actions so the company isn't slowed.

distractors.wrong: A 30% shareholder automatically controls all key decisions
distractors.why: proportional votes don't give control; minority protection covenants grant veto over specified key matters

distractors.wrong: Reserved matters should cover every business decision
distractors.why: keep the list TIGHT to company-critical actions, or the company is paralysed

nodes.sample_question: What are minority-protection covenants / reserved matters, and how are they implemented? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming proportional votes protect a minority, or making the reserved-matters list too broad.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Term sheets lay out EXIT expectations because founders and investors differ: founders may want to build enduring value forever; investors must realise a return within their fund's life. Exits are NATURAL (planned) or EVENT-DRIVEN (e.g. non-compliance forcing an exit). Methods: ACQUISITION/trade sale, IPO, and (less common in India) BUYBACK. Terms include a TIME PERIOD (e.g. 5 years), and options: a PUT option (investor can force the founder/company to buy its shares) — often WITHOUT a reciprocal CALL option for the founder (bargaining power). In the US, mandatory IPO registration rights are common.

distractors.wrong: Founders and investors share the same exit time horizon
distractors.why: investors must exit within their fund's life; founders may want to hold forever

distractors.wrong: A put option always comes with a reciprocal call option for the founder
distractors.why: investors with bargaining power often get a put WITHOUT giving the founder a call

nodes.sample_question: Why do term sheets specify exit terms, and what is an investor put option? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming aligned exit horizons or symmetric put/call options.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Deal-specific conditions protect the investor from circumstances UNIQUE to a transaction, often as CONDITIONS PRECEDENT (CPs) — things that must happen BEFORE the money is released. Example: a cardiology-services start-up run by clinicians must APPOINT a professional CEO as a condition precedent, so the investor isn't funding a company without managerial capacity. Because the term sheet isn't binding, conditioning the actual money release on the CP protects the investor.

distractors.wrong: Conditions precedent are met after the money is invested
distractors.why: CPs must be satisfied BEFORE the investment is released (conditions SUBSEQUENT come after)

distractors.wrong: Deal-specific conditions are standard boilerplate
distractors.why: they address risks UNIQUE to a transaction (e.g. requiring a professional CEO be hired)

nodes.sample_question: What is a condition precedent, illustrated by the clinician-CEO example? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing conditions precedent (before money) with conditions subsequent (after money).

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: A LIQUIDATION PREFERENCE gives the investor PRIORITY in the payout queue (ahead of founders/common holders) when the company is sold/liquidated. The investor CHOOSES the better of: (a) CONVERT to equity and take their %, or (b) exercise the preference and take their money back FIRST, as a MULTIPLE (1x / 1.5x / 2x / 3x). It can be NON-PARTICIPATING (take the multiple OR the %, whichever is higher) or PARTICIPATING (take the multiple AND then share pro-rata in the remainder). It only bites when the company underperforms; in a great exit the investor usually just converts.

distractors.wrong: Liquidation preference gives common shareholders priority
distractors.why: it gives the INVESTOR (preference holder) priority over founders/common holders

distractors.wrong: Participating and non-participating preferences pay the same
distractors.why: non-participating = multiple OR pro-rata (higher); participating = multiple PLUS pro-rata of the remainder

nodes.sample_question: What does a liquidation preference give an investor, and what is the difference between participating and non-participating? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Giving priority to common holders, or conflating participating with non-participating preferences.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.formula: non_participating = max(multiple x investment, ownership_% x proceeds); participating = multiple x investment + ownership_% x (proceeds - multiple x investment)
nodes.teaching_note: The investor picks the option giving the higher payoff. NON-PARTICIPATING payout = max(multiple x investment, ownership% x proceeds). PARTICIPATING payout = multiple x investment + ownership% x (proceeds - multiple x investment). CLA-verified examples: (1) invest Rs 10 cr for 20%, exit Rs 100 cr, 1x PARTICIPATING -> 10 + 0.20 x (100-10) = 10 + 18 = Rs 28 cr; (2) invest Rs 20 cr for 20%, exit Rs 200 cr, 2x NON-participating, optimal -> max(2x20=40, 0.20x200=40) = Rs 40 cr. The investor converts when equity value exceeds the preference and it is non-participating.

distractors.wrong: A participating investor only takes the multiple
distractors.why: participating = multiple PLUS pro-rata of the remainder (e.g. 10 + 0.2x90 = 28, not 10)

distractors.wrong: A non-participating investor always takes the liquidation preference
distractors.why: they take the GREATER of the multiple or converting to equity %; they convert when equity value is higher

nodes.sample_question: An investor puts Rs 10 cr for 20% with a 1x participating preference; the firm exits at Rs 100 cr. What is the payout if they participate? (calculation)
nodes.failure_mode: Forgetting the pro-rata add-on for participating, or not taking the max for non-participating.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: ANTI-DILUTION protection shields an early investor from EXCESSIVE/disproportionate dilution in a DOWN ROUND — a round priced BELOW the previous round's share price (a key consequence of a down round is heavy dilution of the founder's and early investor's stakes). In an UP round (higher price) dilution is normal and uncontentious; the problem is the down round. The protection re-prices the early investor's conversion so they aren't punished for the company's underperformance. It comes in two forms: full ratchet and weighted average.

distractors.wrong: A down round is a round at a higher valuation
distractors.why: a DOWN round is priced LOWER than the previous round (an UP round is higher)

distractors.wrong: Anti-dilution protects against all dilution
distractors.why: it protects only against EXCESSIVE dilution in a DOWN round, not the normal dilution of an up round

nodes.sample_question: What is a down round, and what does anti-dilution protection do? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing down (lower price) with up (higher price) rounds, or thinking anti-dilution stops all dilution.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.concept: Anti-dilution: full ratchet vs weighted average
nodes.formula: full_ratchet: early investor shares = investment / new_low_price; weighted_average: conversion_price between old and new (broad-based < narrow-based protection)
nodes.teaching_note: Two anti-dilution methods. FULL RATCHET: the early investor's conversion price RESETS to the new low (down-round) price (1:1) — maximum protection for them, but harshest on the founder and the new (Series B) investor. WEIGHTED AVERAGE: conversion re-prices to a point BETWEEN the old and new price using a formula; BROAD-BASED (includes options/ESOP/convertibles in the share base) gives LESS protection (more founder-friendly) than NARROW-BASED. Founders and the Series B investor are better off under weighted average than full ratchet; the outcome depends on BARGAINING POWER. CLA-verified full-ratchet cap table: founder Rs 10,00,000 at Re 1; Series A Rs 2,50,000 (20%) at Re 1; Series B Rs 2,00,000 at Re 0.50; full ratchet re-prices Series A to Re 0.50 (5,00,000 shares) -> founder 52.6%, Series A 26.3%, Series B 21.1% (sums to 100%).

distractors.wrong: Broad-based weighted average gives the investor more protection than full ratchet
distractors.why: FULL RATCHET gives the most protection; broad-based weighted average gives the least (most founder-friendly)

distractors.wrong: Under full ratchet the early investor converts at the original price
distractors.why: full ratchet RESETS the conversion price to the new low down-round price (1:1)

nodes.sample_question: Founder holds 10,00,000 shares (Re 1); Series A invested Rs 2,50,000 (Re 1); Series B invests Rs 2,00,000 at Re 0.50 with Series A on full ratchet. Find the new ownership split. (calculation)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing full ratchet (resets to new price) with weighted average, or a cap table not summing to 100%.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: An EXIT is the process by which investors (and founders) DISENGAGE from the investment relationship. It matters for BOTH parties: investors must return capital + return to their limited partners (fixed-life funds) and need liquidity; FOUNDERS need diversification (all their wealth is locked in one company) and liquidity. Exits also VALIDATE the enterprise's financial value and require thinking about the change in ownership. Without reliable exit mechanisms, investors are reluctant to invest. Fund managers face a compulsion to exit to raise their next fund (a source of founder-investor misalignment on timing).

distractors.wrong: Exits matter only to investors
distractors.why: founders also need exits for diversification and liquidity — all their wealth is in one company
