distractors.wrong: Exits are unrelated to whether investors will invest at all
distractors.why: without reliable exit mechanisms, investors are reluctant to invest in a market/geography

nodes.sample_question: Why are exits important to both investors and founders? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Framing exits as an investor-only concern and missing founder diversification.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Major exit routes, most-to-least preferred: (1) IPO (most desirable — capital appreciation, visibility); (2) SECONDARY sale (to another financial investor); (3) TRADE SALE / strategic acquisition (a strategic buyer wants the tech/products/customers); (4) BUYBACK (company or promoter buys the shares back — least common in India); and (5) SELF-LIQUIDATING instruments (preference shares/convertible loans redeemed from cash flow — for underdeveloped markets). Not all routes are available to every company.

distractors.wrong: Buyback is the most preferred exit route
distractors.why: IPO is most preferred; buyback is least common in India

distractors.wrong: Every company can choose any exit route
distractors.why: not all routes are available to every company — e.g. only some qualify for an IPO

nodes.sample_question: List the exit routes in order of preference. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Mis-ordering exit routes or assuming all routes suit all companies.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: An INITIAL PUBLIC OFFERING sells shares to the public on a stock exchange. It is prized for CAPITAL APPRECIATION (thousands of buyers/sellers, no ceiling on the share price) and VISIBILITY/brand (Zomato, Nykaa, Paytm). Price is set via BOOK-BUILDING; investors/founders can sell in an OFFER FOR SALE (OFS) at the IPO price, or in the AFTERMARKET at the trading price. Not every company qualifies — access depends on INVESTOR PREFERENCE (today: tech/IT/healthcare/media over commodity sectors) and meeting SEBI/exchange listing CRITERIA. Any company issuing shares to the public must go through SEBI.

distractors.wrong: IPO shares always sell at the prevailing market price
distractors.why: OFS shares sell at the book-built IPO price; only AFTERMARKET sales use the trading price

distractors.wrong: Every company can do an IPO whenever it wants
distractors.why: only companies meeting SEBI/exchange criteria and investor preference qualify

nodes.sample_question: What makes an IPO attractive, and which regulator must a company issuing shares to the public approach? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing OFS (IPO price) with aftermarket sales, or assuming any firm can IPO.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: An IPO is a HIGHLY REGULATED, costly, time-consuming process. The company prepares a (Draft) RED HERRING PROSPECTUS (RHP, ~450-500 pages) that SEBI must clear (so investors have enough information). A MERCHANT BANKER (mandatory) manages the issue. Executives do a ROADSHOW (sometimes Singapore/London/New York) to market the issue. From board approval to completion takes ~8-12 months and costs ~7-10% of issue proceeds, plus heavy top-management time. After listing, the company faces ongoing governance/disclosure COMPLIANCE and loss of secrecy.

distractors.wrong: A company can IPO within a few weeks
distractors.why: from board decision to completion takes ~8-12 months (prospectus, SEBI clearance, merchant banker, roadshow)

distractors.wrong: Listing reduces a company's compliance and disclosure burden
distractors.why: listed companies face MORE ongoing governance/disclosure compliance and loss of secrecy

nodes.sample_question: What are the main regulatory and operational realities of doing an IPO? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Underestimating IPO time/cost/compliance, or forgetting the merchant-banker/RHP requirements.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: TRADE SALE / STRATEGIC ACQUISITION: a strategic buyer purchases the company (or stake/assets) for STRATEGIC reasons — access to technology, products or customers (e.g. Cisco bolting on start-ups). Strategic acquirers often want majority/100%, triggering a DRAG-ALONG clause to force minority/founder along. SECONDARY PURCHASE: a FINANCIAL investor (VC-like, no strategic motive) buys an EXISTING investor's stake for return. Both typically yield LOWER realisations than an IPO (fewer buyers/negotiation), and founders often LEAVE within a year or two after a strategic sale; deals close fast (a month or less).

distractors.wrong: A secondary purchase is made by a strategic acquirer
distractors.why: a secondary purchase is by a FINANCIAL investor (no strategic motive); a TRADE sale is the strategic one

distractors.wrong: Trade sales fetch higher prices than IPOs
distractors.why: trade sales/secondaries usually realise LESS than IPOs (fewer buyers, private negotiation)

nodes.sample_question: Distinguish a strategic trade sale from a secondary purchase. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing strategic (trade sale) with financial (secondary) buyers, or overrating trade-sale prices.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: A BUYBACK is an exit where the COMPANY or the PROMOTER/founder buys the investor's shares back. Company buyback (more common) usually EXTINGUISHES the shares and is regulated by the Companies Act (Sections 68-69), with a key limit: a company cannot buy back more than 25% of its share capital (so a 30-40% investor can't fully exit via company buyback). Promoter buyback is feasible in two cases: a failed company (investor books a loss to exit) or a parent/foreign promoter wanting to raise control (e.g. from 30% to 51%).

distractors.wrong: A company can buy back any percentage of its shares
distractors.why: a company cannot buy back more than 25% of its share capital (Companies Act)

distractors.wrong: Buyback is the most common exit in India
distractors.why: buyback is the LEAST common/preferred exit route in India

nodes.sample_question: Who buys the shares in a buyback, and what is the Companies Act limit on company buyback? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Ignoring the 25% buyback cap or treating buyback as a primary exit route.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: In markets where IPO/trade-sale/secondary exits are unreliable (underdeveloped financial markets), investors fund via SELF-LIQUIDATING instruments — preference shares or convertible loans REDEEMED from the company's own CASH FLOW rather than via an exit event. If the company is profitable but unlikely to IPO or be acquired, the investor structures funding so it is repaid (e.g. 3-4x over 5 years) from cash flow without needing to convert to equity or find a buyer. Used by investors in underdeveloped markets and developmental institutions.

distractors.wrong: Self-liquidating instruments require an IPO or acquisition to pay out
distractors.why: they are repaid from the company's CASH FLOW, precisely because no exit event is available

distractors.wrong: They are used in highly developed capital markets
distractors.why: they are for UNDERDEVELOPED markets where IPO/trade-sale exits are unreliable

nodes.sample_question: What is a self-liquidating instrument and when is it used? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Thinking self-liquidating instruments need an exit event, or are for developed markets.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Closing perspectives: (1) the course centres on EQUITY, but loans (against collateral) are possible — though risky for start-ups; quasi-equity (preference/convertibles redeemed from cash flow) suits those without an exit path. (2) The early-stage market is largely PRIVATE/opaque — prices, valuations and terms are confidential, so NETWORKING (conferences, peer conversations) is how founders learn shifting preferences/trends. (3) Fundraising is important but NOT the only thing — don't over-optimise dilution at the cost of running the business; given imperfect information you won't always get the best terms, and that's okay.

distractors.wrong: Early-stage funding terms are public and easy to benchmark
distractors.why: the private market is opaque; you learn prices/terms only by networking

distractors.wrong: Founders should maximise time spent optimising fundraising
distractors.why: over-optimising fundraising starves the business; balance it — the day job is the business

nodes.sample_question: What are the key closing lessons on start-up fundraising? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating the private market as transparent or over-investing time in fundraising.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: A start-up pitch packages the company's future prospects into digestible chunks for an investor, tailored to each VC. Core elements: the PROBLEM and customer BENEFIT, MARKET size (TAM/SAM/SOM), COMPETITION and DEFENSIBILITY, UNIT ECONOMICS / realised unit cost, the TEAM, TRACTION/track record (including honest discussion of what deviated from plan — conveying integrity), and the ASK (funding + valuation expectations). A GROWTH/expansion-stage pitch differs from an early-stage one: emphasise headroom for expansion, competition for market share, realised (not pen-and-paper) unit costs, existing investors continuing to back you (the best vote of confidence), and a leadership/staffing plan.

distractors.wrong: The same pitch works for an early-stage and a growth-stage raise
distractors.why: growth-stage pitches emphasise expansion headroom, realised unit costs and existing-investor support — different from early-stage

distractors.wrong: A pitch should hide what went wrong
distractors.why: honestly discussing deviations from plan conveys integrity and reflectiveness to investors

nodes.sample_question: What are the core elements of a start-up pitch, and how does a growth-stage pitch differ? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Reusing an early-stage pitch at growth stage, or hiding setbacks instead of showing integrity.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: India offers four main structures: SOLE PROPRIETORSHIP, PARTNERSHIP FIRM, LLP, and PRIVATE LIMITED COMPANY (plus public company). The choice (hard to pivot later) drives LIABILITY, taxation, compliance, FUNDING options, governance and succession. Decision drivers: liability exposure (limited vs unlimited), growth/FUNDRAISING ambition (companies win for equity raises), foreign money (FEMA is clearer for companies), compliance burden (proprietorship lightest, company heaviest), taxation, and longevity/transferability (LLPs/companies have perpetual succession). For repeated equity fundraising and external investors, the private limited company is the winner.

distractors.wrong: The business structure is easy to change later
distractors.why: it is difficult to pivot structures midway; choose deliberately upfront

distractors.wrong: All structures are equally good for raising equity from investors
distractors.why: the private limited company is built for equity fundraising; proprietorships/partnerships deter investors

nodes.sample_question: What factors drive the choice of business structure, and which suits repeated equity fundraising? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating structure as easily changeable, or thinking any structure suits VC fundraising.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: A SOLE PROPRIETORSHIP is the simplest form: the business and the proprietor are the SAME person, with NO separate legal status and UNLIMITED personal liability for business debts. It is cheap/easy (basic GST/Shops-Establishment registration), and income is taxed as the individual's income. Drawbacks: low credibility with large clients, can't raise funds beyond personal/bank finance (equity investors won't back it), and NO perpetual succession (ends if the proprietor retires/dies). Suitable only for testing ideas / minimum viable product, not for funded ventures.

distractors.wrong: A sole proprietorship has limited liability
distractors.why: it has UNLIMITED personal liability — the proprietor and business are the same person

distractors.wrong: A sole proprietorship can raise equity from investors
distractors.why: it cannot — equity investors won't back it; financing is limited to personal/bank finance

nodes.sample_question: What are the defining features and limits of a sole proprietorship? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Attributing limited liability or investability to a sole proprietorship.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: A PARTNERSHIP FIRM (Indian Partnership Act, 1932) is owned by 2-20 partners under a PARTNERSHIP DEED (roles, capital, profit-sharing, dispute resolution). It has NO separate legal identity and UNLIMITED liability (personal assets settle business debts), though risk is shared across partners. Registration with the Registrar of Firms is OPTIONAL but recommended (an UNREGISTERED firm cannot sue third parties or claim set-off). Compliance is light. Like a sole proprietorship, it struggles with credibility, investability and ownership transfer, so external/strategic investors avoid it.

distractors.wrong: A partnership firm has a separate legal identity from its partners
distractors.why: it has NO separate legal identity and unlimited liability; an LLP/company has separate identity

distractors.wrong: Partnership firm registration is mandatory
distractors.why: registration is OPTIONAL (but recommended; an unregistered firm cannot sue third parties)

nodes.sample_question: What governs a partnership firm, and what is the consequence of not registering it? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Attributing separate legal identity to a partnership, or thinking registration is mandatory.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: An LLP (LLP Act, 2008) is a HYBRID of a partnership and a company: a SEPARATE LEGAL ENTITY (distinct from its partners) with LIMITED LIABILITY restricted to each partner's capital contribution (unless fraud/wrongful acts). It can own property and sue independently, is registered with the MCA (name via RUN-LLP, incorporation via FiLLiP, LLP agreement via Form 3 within 30 days), and has lighter compliance than a company, with no maximum number of partners. Best for professional-services/medium-risk ventures; raising equity from formal investors is challenging (no shares to issue). An LLP does NOT require an AGM.

distractors.wrong: An LLP has unlimited liability like a partnership firm
distractors.why: an LLP gives LIMITED liability (capped at contribution) and is a separate legal entity

distractors.wrong: An LLP must hold an Annual General Meeting
distractors.why: an AGM is NOT required for an LLP (it is required for a company)

nodes.sample_question: Which Act governs an LLP, and how does its liability differ from a partnership firm? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating an LLP like an unlimited-liability partnership, or requiring an AGM for it.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: A PRIVATE LIMITED COMPANY (Companies Act, 2013) is a SEPARATE LEGAL ENTITY run by a board of directors, with shareholders' liability LIMITED to unpaid share capital (the corporate veil is pierced only for fraud). It offers high credibility, transferability, PERPETUAL succession, and the cleanest route to raise from angels/VCs/foreign investors — but the HEAVIEST compliance burden (annual filings, registers, audits). Maximum 200 shareholders (beyond that it becomes a public company). Charter documents: MOA (bones/scope) and AOA (internal rules/running). It is the standard vehicle for funded start-ups.

distractors.wrong: A private limited company can have unlimited shareholders
distractors.why: it is capped at 200 shareholders; beyond that it becomes a public company

distractors.wrong: Shareholders are personally liable for all company debts
distractors.why: liability is LIMITED to unpaid share capital (the veil lifts only for fraud)

nodes.sample_question: Which Act governs a private limited company, and what is its shareholder cap and liability? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Forgetting the 200-shareholder cap or the limited-liability principle.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: A ONE PERSON COMPANY (OPC) is a private company with a SINGLE member, enjoying SEPARATE legal status and PERPETUAL succession (unlike a sole proprietorship). It can be incorporated by an Indian citizen (resident or NRI). It gives a solo founder limited liability and a corporate identity, but cannot carry out non-banking financial (NBFC) activities and is not a Section 8 (not-for-profit) form. It bridges the gap between a sole proprietorship (no separate status) and a multi-member private company.

distractors.wrong: An OPC is the same as a sole proprietorship
distractors.why: an OPC has SEPARATE legal status and perpetual succession; a sole proprietorship has neither

distractors.wrong: An OPC needs at least two members
distractors.why: an OPC has a SINGLE member by definition

nodes.sample_question: How does a One Person Company differ from a sole proprietorship? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Equating an OPC (separate entity, limited liability) with a sole proprietorship.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: The two charter/constitutional documents of a company: the MEMORANDUM OF ASSOCIATION (MOA) defines the company's SCOPE and objectives — name, state, registered-office, capital and liability clauses (the 'bones'); the ARTICLES OF ASSOCIATION (AOA) govern INTERNAL management and running — shareholder rights, board powers, how shares are issued, director appointments, meetings (the 'rules'). Investors often insist a SHAREHOLDERS' AGREEMENT be incorporated into the AOA (since the AOA can supersede a standalone agreement). Both can be altered via Companies Act 2013 procedures.

distractors.wrong: The Articles of Association defines the company's scope and objectives
distractors.why: the MOA defines scope/objectives; the AOA governs internal management/rules

distractors.wrong: MOA and AOA cover the same aspects
distractors.why: MOA = scope/external boundaries; AOA = internal running rules — they are distinct

nodes.sample_question: Which document defines a company's scope and objectives, and which governs its internal management? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Swapping the roles of the MOA (scope) and AOA (internal rules).

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Incorporating a company/LLP online requires: a DIGITAL SIGNATURE CERTIFICATE (DSC — valid under the IT Act, in a USB token, for online MCA filings); a DIRECTOR IDENTIFICATION NUMBER (DIN — 8-digit, lifetime, via Form DIR-3, KYC every year by June, max 3 directors at incorporation); a REGISTERED OFFICE (intimated via INC-22 within 30 days); and charter documents (MOA/AOA). A company files SPICe+ (Part A name, Part B + AGILE-PRO) at the MCA; an LLP files RUN-LLP (name) and FiLLiP. The Certificate of Incorporation issues with PAN/TAN/ESIC/EPF.

distractors.wrong: A Digital Signature Certificate is mainly for paying salaries online
distractors.why: the DSC is primarily for ONLINE FILING of documents with the MCA

distractors.wrong: A DIN is obtained fresh for every filing
distractors.why: a DIN is allotted once and is for the director's lifetime (with periodic KYC)

nodes.sample_question: What is a Digital Signature Certificate primarily required for in incorporation? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Misattributing the purpose of the DSC/DIN in the incorporation process.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: After incorporation a company must: hold a BOARD MEETING within 30 days; open a bank account and file INC-20A (commencement of business) before borrowing/operating; issue SHARE CERTIFICATES within 60 days of allotment; maintain a Statutory Register of Members; appoint an AUDITOR within 30 days (board) — filing ADT-1 within 15 days; and obtain business registrations. Companies must hold an ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING (the first within 9 months of the first financial-year close, then within 6 months) — an AGM is mandatory for a private limited company, NOT for an LLP, partnership or proprietorship.

distractors.wrong: Share certificates can be issued any time after incorporation
distractors.why: they must be issued within 60 days of allotment (and stamped within 2 months)

distractors.wrong: An AGM is mandatory for an LLP
distractors.why: an AGM is mandatory for a COMPANY, not for an LLP/partnership/proprietorship

nodes.sample_question: For which entity is an Annual General Meeting mandatory, and what is the share-certificate timeline? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Requiring an AGM for an LLP, or missing the 30/60-day post-incorporation timelines.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: DPIIT (start-up) registration is NOT mandatory but unlocks benefits. Eligibility: any entity except a sole proprietorship, turnover < Rs 100 cr, working towards innovation/IP, valid 10 years from incorporation; NOT available to an entity formed by splitting/reconstruction. BENEFITS: self-certification on labour/IP laws (reduced fees, fast-track patents), ability to issue CONVERTIBLE NOTES, issue ESOPs to PROMOTERS (otherwise barred), exemption from the 100%-of-capital borrowing cap (for 5 years), raise deposits from shareholders without limit, and Income-Tax benefits (carry-forward of losses, tax holidays).

distractors.wrong: DPIIT registration is mandatory and primarily for early tax payment
distractors.why: it is OPTIONAL; its purpose is start-up RECOGNITION and access to government benefits, not paying tax early

distractors.wrong: A company formed by splitting an existing business can register as a start-up
distractors.why: entities formed by splitting/reconstruction are NOT eligible for DPIIT start-up recognition

nodes.sample_question: What is DPIIT registration primarily for, and name two benefits it confers. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Thinking DPIIT registration is mandatory/tax-related, or that split entities qualify.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: MSME registration (via the UDYAM portal — one-time, free, no renewal) classifies manufacturing/trading/service entities as MICRO, SMALL or MEDIUM by investment in plant/machinery and annual turnover. Benefits: easier/cheaper LOANS (reduced interest), subsidies for patents/trademarks/standardisation, and — importantly — a 45-DAY payment protection: buyers must pay MSME dues within 45 days, with delays reportable to the Ministry (Form MSME-1). Other common registrations: bank account, ESIC/EPFO, GST (above a turnover threshold), Shops & Establishment, professional tax, Factories Act (manufacturing), IEC (import-export), POSH (SHe-Box).

distractors.wrong: MSME registration is costly and must be renewed annually
distractors.why: UDYAM registration is FREE, one-time, with no renewal

distractors.wrong: MSME buyers can pay dues whenever they like
distractors.why: MSME dues must be paid within 45 days; delays are reportable via Form MSME-1

nodes.sample_question: What does MSME (UDYAM) registration provide, including the payment-protection rule? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Thinking MSME registration is costly/renewable or that the 45-day rule doesn't apply.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: GOVERNANCE hierarchy: shareholders are the supreme body -> delegate to the BOARD of directors -> who authorise the MD/CEO -> CXOs run functions. ROUTINE company compliance: minimum 4 BOARD MEETINGS/year (<=120 days apart); AGM (first within 9 months of FY close, then 6 months); file financials (AOC-4, 30 days) and annual return (MGT-7, 60 days after AGM); DIR-3 KYC; Form MSME-1 (dues > 45 days); DPT-3 (deposits, by June); PAS-6 (demat, half-yearly). EVENT-BASED compliance triggers on auditor/capital/office changes. LLPs have lighter compliance. Non-compliance carries penalties and harms future fundraising credibility.

distractors.wrong: Companies need only one board meeting a year
distractors.why: a company needs a MINIMUM of 4 board meetings a year, no more than 120 days apart

distractors.wrong: LLPs and companies have the same compliance burden
distractors.why: LLPs have LIGHTER compliance than companies

nodes.sample_question: What is the governance hierarchy, and how many board meetings must a company hold per year? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Understating board-meeting frequency or equating LLP and company compliance.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Shareholder decisions are passed by RESOLUTIONS at a general meeting. An ORDINARY resolution needs a SIMPLE majority (>50%); a SPECIAL resolution needs a 75% majority. Major fundraising actions — private placement / preferential allotment, increasing authorised capital, issuing convertible notes, amending the AOA — require a SPECIAL resolution. Special resolutions are filed with the Registrar of Companies in Form MGT-14 (typically within 30 days) for transparency/public record.

distractors.wrong: A special resolution needs a simple majority
distractors.why: a special resolution needs 75%; an ORDINARY resolution needs a simple majority (>50%)

distractors.wrong: Raising funds via private placement needs only an ordinary resolution
distractors.why: private placement / preferential allotment requires a SPECIAL resolution (75%)

nodes.sample_question: What majority does a special resolution require, and which fundraising actions need one? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing the thresholds (ordinary >50% vs special 75%) or the actions requiring each.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Funding stages with their typical sources: PRE-SEED (ideas/prototype — family/friends, grants, B-plan competitions/hackathons, collateral-free); SEED (MVP/launch — angels, HNIs, family offices, networks); SERIES A (product-market fit, scaling — institutional VC funds registered with SEBI); SERIES B/C (growth, rising revenue — PE/growth-equity firms); SERIES D/E/F (expansion); then EXIT via acquisition or IPO. Angel investors are the most suitable source for the PROOF-OF-CONCEPT stage (banks/IPO are not).

distractors.wrong: Bank loans or an IPO suit the proof-of-concept stage
distractors.why: the PoC stage suits ANGEL investors; banks rarely lend to start-ups and IPO needs scale/compliance

distractors.wrong: Series A is typically funded by family and friends
distractors.why: Series A is funded by institutional VC funds; family/friends fund pre-seed

nodes.sample_question: Which funding source is most suitable for the proof-of-concept stage of a high-risk start-up? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Matching the wrong source to a stage (e.g. banks/IPO for proof-of-concept).

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.concept: Sources of funding: equity, debt, grants
nodes.teaching_note: Funding sources fall into: EQUITY capital (permanent, highest risk, residual claim, voting, dividend after preference); PREFERENCE capital (preference on dividend, stated coupon rate); DEBT capital (borrowings from directors/relatives/shareholders, inter-corporate, banks, PE; instruments include convertible notes and CCDs); and GRANTS (B-plan competitions, government R&D in education/defence/semiconductors/health/AI, incubators, IMPACT INVESTORS who weigh social impact alongside returns). Each grant/source has terms/conditions to adhere to.

distractors.wrong: Equity shareholders are paid before preference shareholders
distractors.why: equity is the residual claimant — paid AFTER preference shareholders; it bears highest risk

distractors.wrong: Grants are a typical ongoing funding-pipeline source
distractors.why: grants (competitions, government R&D, impact investors) are special-purpose, not a typical funding pipeline

nodes.sample_question: Name the categories of funding sources and where equity sits in the payment hierarchy. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Putting equity ahead of preference in the payout queue, or treating grants as routine funding.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Under the Companies Act, a private company may borrow from SHAREHOLDERS up to 100% of (paid-up capital + free reserves + securities premium) — but a DPIIT-registered start-up is EXEMPT from this cap for 5 years. Loans from DIRECTORS are an 'EXEMPTED DEPOSIT' (board approval + a director declaration that funds aren't borrowed/laundered, no specific limit), reported annually in Form DPT-3. A company CANNOT borrow from friends/family (unless they become shareholders, or it's an exempted category) or take public deposits; bank loans and inter-corporate loans are allowed. Advances against supply must be adjusted within ~11 months or become a deposit.

distractors.wrong: A start-up can freely borrow from friends and family
distractors.why: borrowing from friends/family is generally NOT allowed unless they become shareholders or it's an exempt category

distractors.wrong: Director loans count toward the 100%-of-capital borrowing cap
distractors.why: director loans are an EXEMPTED DEPOSIT (no limit, board approval + declaration); the cap is on shareholder borrowings

nodes.sample_question: Up to what limit can a private company borrow from shareholders, and how are director loans treated? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Allowing friends/family loans, or applying the borrowing cap to director loans.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: A RIGHTS ISSUE offers new shares to EXISTING shareholders in PROPORTION to their holdings (preserving their %, a fundamental governance right). Process: board resolution -> offer letter; the offer stays open a minimum of 7 and maximum of 30 days; each shareholder may ACCEPT, DECLINE, or RENOUNCE (transfer the right to another); SILENCE = decline. Shares must be allotted within 60 days of receiving application money; file PAS-3 with the RoC within 30 days; issue stamped share certificates within 2 months. Non-resident participation triggers FEMA/RBI reporting.

distractors.wrong: A rights issue brings in new outside investors
distractors.why: a rights issue offers shares to EXISTING shareholders pro-rata; preferential allotment/private placement brings in new investors

distractors.wrong: Shareholder silence counts as acceptance of a rights issue
distractors.why: silence = DECLINE; the shareholder must actively accept and remit money

nodes.sample_question: To whom is a rights issue offered, and what are a shareholder's three options? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing a rights issue (existing holders) with private placement (new investors), or treating silence as acceptance.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: When existing shareholders can't fund the round, a private company raises from IDENTIFIED outside investors via PREFERENTIAL ALLOTMENT / PRIVATE PLACEMENT (a private company can't make a public issue). Instruments: equity shares, CCPS (Compulsory Convertible Preference Shares), CCD (Compulsory Convertible Debenture), or OCD. Pre-checks: sufficient AUTHORISED share capital (increase if needed), a separate/ESCROW bank account for application money, and a VALUATION report by a registered valuer (90-day validity; merchant banker for non-residents). Process: board approval -> SPECIAL resolution -> file MGT-14 (30 days) -> offer letter PAS-4 (named to each investor) -> allotment within 60 days -> file PAS-3 within 15 days.

distractors.wrong: Preferential allotment requires only an ordinary resolution and no valuation
distractors.why: it needs a SPECIAL resolution (75%) and a registered-valuer valuation report

distractors.wrong: Private placement can be offered to the general public
distractors.why: a private company can only offer to IDENTIFIED investors (named PAS-4), not the public

nodes.sample_question: How does a private company raise from new identified investors, and what pre-checks are required? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Skipping the valuation/special-resolution requirements, or offering private placement to the public.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: A CONVERTIBLE NOTE (introduced 2016, available ONLY to DPIIT-registered start-ups) is a hybrid debt instrument with an option to CONVERT to equity (or be repaid) within 10 years of issuance. Minimum ticket size is Rs 25 lakh per single investor (3 friends each putting Rs ~8 lakh don't qualify — they'd need to be a consortium/AIF/single Rs 25 lakh+ investor). KEY ADVANTAGE: NO valuation report is needed at issue (valuation is deferred to conversion) and compliance is lighter (board + special resolution + MGT-14 + CN certificate + RBI for non-residents) — making it the preferred instrument when funds are needed URGENTLY on a short timeline. Conversion is often at a DISCOUNT at the next qualified round.

distractors.wrong: Any start-up can issue a convertible note for any amount
distractors.why: only DPIIT-registered start-ups can, with a minimum of Rs 25 lakh per single investor

distractors.wrong: A convertible note requires a valuation report at issue
distractors.why: NO valuation is needed at issue (deferred to conversion) — a key reason it's used for urgent funding

nodes.sample_question: Who can issue a convertible note, what is the minimum ticket size, and why is no valuation needed at issue? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Allowing non-DPIIT start-ups or sub-Rs 25 lakh tickets, or requiring valuation at issue.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: DUE DILIGENCE is the investor's pre-investment 'health check' (after the term sheet, during the ~90-day non-binding period). FINANCIAL DD (CAs verify books, GST/TDS, the real financial condition vs the rosy deck); LEGAL DD checks corporate records/filings, regulatory COMPLIANCE (Companies Act, FEMA, labour, tax, IP, IT/DPDP, sector licences — FSSAI/IRDA/RBI/TRAI), IP STATUS (valuation often rests on IP), hidden/fraudulent transactions, tax DUES, litigation, and contracts. Purpose = price the RISK (and offset it in valuation or via safeguards), NOT to embarrass. A data room/checklist is used; magnitude scales with stage (angel basic -> Series A/B/C stringent). Findings feed conditions precedent/subsequent.

distractors.wrong: Due diligence happens after the money is invested
distractors.why: DD is a PRE-investment activity (after the term sheet, before the money)

distractors.wrong: The purpose of DD is to embarrass the founder
distractors.why: its purpose is to price/understand RISK and offset it in valuation or via safeguards

nodes.sample_question: When does due diligence happen and what does it cover? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Treating DD as post-investment or punitive rather than pre-investment risk pricing.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: DD findings produce a REPORT splitting fixes into CONDITIONS PRECEDENT (before money) and CONDITIONS SUBSEQUENT (after, time-bound), and feed the share subscription/shareholders agreement via REPRESENTATIONS & WARRANTIES and INDEMNIFICATION. RED FLAGS (from live cases like GCL Technologies): no statutory records/minutes, unrecorded promoter loans, unregistered IP (pulls valuation down), share certificates not issued, auditor not appointed, director loans unreported, and director DISQUALIFICATION. Consequences: lower valuation, delayed or DENIED investment, walk-away. Penalties are NOT tax-deductible. Non-compliance also surfaces in the auditor's public report, hurting credibility.

distractors.wrong: DD red flags have no effect on valuation or the deal
distractors.why: red flags lower valuation, delay/deny the investment, or cause walk-away

distractors.wrong: Compliance penalties can be deducted as a business expense
distractors.why: penalties are NOT allowed as business expenditure (not deductible)

nodes.sample_question: What are common due-diligence red flags and their consequences? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Underrating how non-compliance red flags depress valuation or kill a deal.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Funding closes in three phases: CONDITIONS PRECEDENT (CP — before money: government/shareholder approvals, corporate cleanup, valuation report, board/shareholder resolutions, AoA amendment, ancillary docs like employment/IP-assignment, plus a satisfaction letter); CLOSING ACTIONS (disclosure letter, warranties, funds into the company account, board approves allotment, share certificates issued); CONDITIONS SUBSEQUENT (CS — after money, time-bound: rectify DD findings via adjudication/compounding, updated employment agreements, insurance). For non-residents, file FC-GPR with the RBI within 30 days (FEMA). Then start planning the NEXT round — fundraising is a continuous journey, not a destination.

distractors.wrong: Conditions subsequent must be completed before the money is released
distractors.why: CONDITIONS PRECEDENT come before money; conditions SUBSEQUENT are completed after, time-bound

distractors.wrong: Funding closure is the end of the fundraising journey
distractors.why: it's a continuous journey — after closing, planning for the next round begins

nodes.sample_question: What are conditions precedent, closing actions and conditions subsequent in funding closure? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing CP (before money) with CS (after money), or treating closing as the end.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: After DD, the 3-page term sheet becomes ~100-page binding agreements. The SHAREHOLDERS' AGREEMENT (SHA) is the rulebook for the founder-investor relationship (rights, governance, exits, conflict resolution). The SHARE SUBSCRIPTION AGREEMENT (SSA) covers an investor subscribing to NEW shares; the SHARE PURCHASE AGREEMENT (SPA) covers buying EXISTING shares from a seller. Common clauses: REPRESENTATIONS & WARRANTIES (truthful promises; breach -> indemnify), COVENANTS (forward-looking promises, e.g. no new loans without consent), and CONDITIONS PRECEDENT / SUBSEQUENT. Crucially, the AOA SUPERSEDES the SHA, so SHA provisions must be incorporated into the AOA or they are toothless.

distractors.wrong: A share subscription agreement covers buying existing shares from a seller
distractors.why: the SSA covers subscribing to NEW shares; the SPA covers buying EXISTING shares

distractors.wrong: A shareholders' agreement automatically overrides the Articles
distractors.why: the AOA SUPERSEDES the SHA — SHA terms must be written into the AOA to be enforceable

nodes.sample_question: Distinguish the SHA, SSA and SPA, and explain why SHA terms must go into the AOA. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing SSA (new shares) with SPA (existing shares), or assuming the SHA overrides the AOA.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Share-transfer restrictions control who can sell to whom. RIGHT OF FIRST REFUSAL (ROFR): a seller must first get a market offer, then offer the shares to the ROFR holder at that price. RIGHT OF FIRST OFFER (ROFO): the seller first asks the ROFO holder for a price, then may test the market. Investors prefer ROFR (no price-discovery cost). TAG-ALONG: lets a minority holder JOIN a sale to a third party on the same terms (protects minority). DRAG-ALONG: lets a majority/investor FORCE other shareholders to sell into a third-party deal (enables a clean 100% sale).

distractors.wrong: Tag-along and drag-along rights do the same thing
distractors.why: TAG-along lets a minority JOIN a sale; DRAG-along lets the majority FORCE others to sell

distractors.wrong: Under ROFR the holder names a price first
distractors.why: under ROFR the seller gets a MARKET price first, then offers it to the holder; under ROFO the holder names a price first

nodes.sample_question: Distinguish ROFR from ROFO, and tag-along from drag-along rights. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Swapping ROFR/ROFO mechanics or tag-along (join) with drag-along (force).

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: VENTURE CAPITAL is high-risk, high-reward EQUITY for young companies (it backs ideas/people, not collateral, filling the gap banks won't). In India VC funds are ALTERNATIVE INVESTMENT FUNDS (AIFs) regulated by SEBI; early-stage VC is CATEGORY I AIF (early-stage/SME/socially-beneficial/innovation). Rules: minimum Rs 5 cr fund corpus, minimum ~Rs 5 lakh from an investor, at least 2/3 of corpus in UNLISTED equity, and no more than 25% of corpus in a single company. Capital comes from LIMITED PARTNERS (institutions, sovereign funds, DFIs, family offices). Funds earn a MANAGEMENT FEE (~2%) plus CARRIED INTEREST (~20% of profits/'carry'). SEBI-registered VC funds get pass-through taxation.

distractors.wrong: AIFs are regulated by the RBI and can invest mostly in listed companies
distractors.why: AIFs are regulated by SEBI; a Cat I VC AIF must hold >=2/3 in UNLISTED equity

distractors.wrong: A VC fund can put its whole corpus into one promising company
distractors.why: no more than 25% of the corpus may go into a single company (risk spreading)

nodes.sample_question: Which regulator and AIF category govern early-stage VC funds, and what are the key investment limits? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Attributing AIF regulation to RBI, or missing the 25%/single-company and 2/3-unlisted limits.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Each rung of the funding ladder trades off control, dilution and obligations. ANGELS back the earliest stage with simple governance and mentorship (don't chase money back). VCs write bigger cheques but demand structured governance (board seats, reporting, protective rights). DEBT avoids dilution but adds repayment pressure and may need collateral. STRATEGIC investors add credibility/market access but create operational dependencies (e.g. a clause to source/sell only through them) and may aim to acquire. NEGOTIATING POWER flips toward the founder at the GROWTH stage (proven product) and toward investors early. Founders should pick based on growth plans and willingness to share control.

distractors.wrong: Debt financing dilutes the founder's ownership
distractors.why: DEBT avoids dilution (no shares given up) but adds repayment pressure

distractors.wrong: Investors always hold the negotiating power
distractors.why: negotiating power flips toward the FOUNDER at the growth stage with a proven product

nodes.sample_question: Compare angels, VCs, debt and strategic investors on dilution, control and obligations. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Thinking debt dilutes equity, or that founders never gain negotiating leverage.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: An ESOP gives EMPLOYEES the RIGHT to BUY a set number of company shares at a future date at a PREDETERMINED price — a NON-CASH incentive to attract/retain talent. ELIGIBLE: permanent employees and directors (including of holding/subsidiary). NOT eligible (under the Companies Act): the PROMOTER group, INDEPENDENT directors, and directors holding > 10% equity — UNLESS the company is a DPIIT-registered start-up (exempt for 10 years). Key terms: OPTION (the right), GRANT/EXERCISE PRICE (set by the board, can be below fair value), VESTING period (minimum 1-year cooling from grant), EXERCISE. Lifecycle: GRANT -> VEST -> EXERCISE -> SELL. Compliance: board + special resolution + MGT-14 (+ RBI for non-resident employees).

distractors.wrong: ESOPs can be freely granted to promoters and independent directors
distractors.why: they are barred to promoters/independent directors/>10% holders — UNLESS a DPIIT start-up (exempt 10 yrs)

distractors.wrong: Options vest and can be exercised immediately on grant
distractors.why: a minimum 1-year cooling/vesting period applies from the grant date before conversion

nodes.sample_question: Who is eligible for ESOPs (and who isn't), and what is the ESOP lifecycle? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Granting ESOPs to promoters/independent directors (non-DPIIT), or ignoring the vesting cooling period.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Contracts (under the Indian Contract Act, 1872) are the backbone of commercial relationships; founders must understand key CLAUSES: SCOPE/deliverables (precise, not 'best efforts'); PAYMENT terms (invoicing, due dates, late penalties — protect cash flow); LIABILITY/INDEMNITY (negotiate a CAP linked to fees — avoid unlimited liability that could be a catastrophic payout); CONFIDENTIALITY (survives termination); TERMINATION (notice, fees, auto-renewal); and GOVERNING LAW/JURISDICTION + ARBITRATION (an Indian company should choose Indian law/jurisdiction — easier to fight on home ground). Golden rule: if a clause can be read two ways, assume the worst. Negotiate the points of business value (ownership, payment, liability, termination, IP), not trivia.

distractors.wrong: Founders should accept unlimited liability clauses to win the deal
distractors.why: negotiate a liability CAP linked to fees; unlimited liability can be a catastrophic, company-killing payout

distractors.wrong: A foreign governing-law clause is best for an Indian start-up
distractors.why: an Indian company should choose Indian law/jurisdiction — fighting on home ground is easier/cheaper

nodes.sample_question: Which contract clauses most affect a start-up's risk, and how should liability be handled? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Accepting unlimited liability or a foreign jurisdiction clause without negotiation.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Four IP pillars in India: (1) TRADEMARK (Trade Marks Act, 1999) protects BRAND identity — name, logo, tagline, distinctive colours/shapes; first-to-use, but registration helps; renew every 10 years. (2) COPYRIGHT (Copyright Act, 1957) protects CREATIVE expression — code, designs, content; the CREATOR is the first owner, so an employee/contractor owns their code UNLESS an IP-ASSIGNMENT clause assigns it to the company; automatic, registration strengthens enforceability. (3) PATENT (Patents Act, 1970) protects NOVEL, inventive INVENTIONS (deep tech/biotech); NO patents for pure algorithms/business methods without technical applicability; a provisional patent secures a priority date. (4) DESIGN (Designs Act, 2000) protects the VISUAL appearance/AESTHETICS of a product (not function). Always put IP-assignment clauses in employment/contractor agreements.

distractors.wrong: A patent protects a company's brand name and logo
distractors.why: a TRADEMARK protects brand name/logo; a PATENT protects a novel invention

distractors.wrong: Code written by an employee automatically belongs to the company
distractors.why: the CREATOR is the first owner; the company needs an IP-ASSIGNMENT clause to own it

nodes.sample_question: A bottle maker creates a uniquely shaped bottle with a distinct look and feel. Which IP protection is most appropriate? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing the four IP pillars (e.g. design for aesthetics vs patent for invention vs trademark for brand).

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Core labour compliance for start-ups: SHOPS & ESTABLISHMENTS registration (state-specific — governs working hours, leave, holidays); MANDATORY written appointment letters/employment agreements (roles, compensation, confidentiality, IP assignment, notice, termination); GRATUITY (Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 — applies at >=10 employees; payable after 5 years' service); POSH (Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013 — written policy + Internal Complaints Committee + annual filings, at >=10 employees); and working-hours/overtime/leave rules. India is consolidating ~29 laws into 4 LABOUR CODES (Code on Wages, Industrial Relations Code, Social Security Code, Occupational Safety Health & Working Conditions Code). NON-COMPETE clauses are generally unenforceable in India.

distractors.wrong: Non-compete clauses are fully enforceable against employees in India
distractors.why: post-employment non-competes are generally UNENFORCEABLE in India; use notice periods/non-solicitation instead

distractors.wrong: Gratuity applies from the first employee
distractors.why: the Payment of Gratuity Act applies at >=10 employees and after 5 years' service

nodes.sample_question: Name the key labour-law obligations for an Indian start-up and the four labour codes. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming non-competes are enforceable, or misstating the gratuity/POSH thresholds.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Corporate governance is about TRUST and how a company makes decisions, shares information, handles conflicts and protects value — it applies to ANY company with more than one stakeholder, not just big firms. The control pillars: INFORMATION rights (monitor, not manage), BOARD composition (director vs observer; nominee directors owe fiduciary duty to the COMPANY), and RESERVED MATTERS (a 'don't touch without permission' list — issuing shares, board changes, amending AOA/MOA, borrowing above limits, selling major assets — kept TIGHT so the company isn't slowed). Good governance prevents misunderstandings, protects value and keeps decisions transparent and accountable.

distractors.wrong: Corporate governance matters only for large listed companies
distractors.why: it matters for ANY company with more than one stakeholder, including early start-ups

distractors.wrong: A reserved-matters list should be as long as possible
distractors.why: keep it TIGHT to company-critical actions; an overlong list paralyses the company

nodes.sample_question: Why does corporate governance matter even for a small start-up, and what are its control pillars? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Dismissing governance as a big-company concern, or over-broadening reserved matters.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Beyond control rights, investors negotiate ECONOMIC rights (about MONEY): (1) PRE-EMPTIVE right — the right to participate PRO-RATA in a fresh issuance to prevent dilution (sometimes on better/first terms); (2) ANTI-DILUTION — protection in a down round (full ratchet vs broad/narrow-based weighted average); (3) LIQUIDATION PREFERENCE — priority payout (1x/1.5x/2x, participating vs non-participating); (4) EXIT rights — strategic sale, buyback, plus DRAG-along (majority forces a sale) and TAG-along (minority joins a sale). These determine the payout hierarchy and protect cap tables.

distractors.wrong: Pre-emptive rights let investors block all new share issuances
distractors.why: a pre-emptive right lets an investor PARTICIPATE pro-rata to avoid dilution, not veto issuance

distractors.wrong: Economic rights and control rights are the same
distractors.why: economic rights concern MONEY (pre-emptive/anti-dilution/liquidation/exit); control rights concern decisions/votes

nodes.sample_question: List the main economic rights of shareholders and what each protects. (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing economic rights (money) with control rights, or misreading pre-emptive rights.

nodes.subject: GER
nodes.teaching_note: Real Indian disputes show governance failures destroy value. TATA-MISTRY: a control-vs-process clash — the Supreme Court upheld the chairman's removal, ruling boards are free to make commercial decisions IF procedures are followed (control of PROCESS matters, not just outcome). FORTIS HEALTHCARE: related-party transactions to promoter-linked entities collapsed governance -> auditors resigned, lenders revolted, SEBI acted, valuation collapsed (a board is custodian of shareholder money; RPTs must be transparent, approved, arm's-length). ZEE-SONY: a merger died because conditions precedent weren't met amid mistrust and weak controls. Lesson: good governance is for ANY multi-stakeholder company; the typical start-up dispute arc runs information rights -> boardroom friction -> anti-dilution -> exit-rights fights.

distractors.wrong: The Tata-Mistry ruling was about who was commercially right
distractors.why: the court focused on PROCESS — boards may make commercial decisions if procedures are followed

distractors.wrong: Related-party transactions are fine if the promoter approves them
distractors.why: RPTs must be transparent, board-approved and arm's-length; opaque RPTs collapsed Fortis

nodes.sample_question: What governance lessons come from the Tata-Mistry, Fortis and Zee-Sony disputes? (concept)
nodes.failure_mode: Reading governance disputes as about being 'right' rather than about process/transparency.
